nodes.title: C++ Basics (1/2)
intro:
**What is undefined behavior?**

Code the standard places no requirements on: the compiler may assume it never happens, so anything can occur (crash, wrong output, or apparently fine). Examples: out-of-bounds access, null dereference, signed overflow, reading uninitialized memory, data races.

nodes.title: C++ Basics (2/2)
intro:
**How do you pass a large object to a function efficiently?**

By `const` reference if the function only reads it, to avoid a copy. By non-const reference if it must modify the caller's object.

nodes.title: Pointers and References (1/3)
intro:
**Pointer vs reference?**

A pointer holds an address, can be null, can be re-pointed, and needs `*` to use. A reference is a permanent alias that must be initialized and cannot be null. Use references for parameters, pointers when "nothing" is a valid value or you need to re-point.

**Stack vs heap?**

The stack holds locals and is freed automatically when the scope ends; it is fast but small. The heap holds `new`-allocated objects that live until you free them; it is large but slower and you must manage the lifetime (or let a smart pointer do it).

nodes.title: Pointers and References (2/3)
intro:
**What is a dangling pointer?**

A pointer to memory that has been freed or has gone out of scope. Dereferencing it is undefined behavior. Setting a pointer to `nullptr` after `delete` helps, and smart pointers avoid the problem.

**`const int*` vs `int* const`?**

Read right to left. `const int*` is a pointer to a const int (data is read-only, pointer can move). `int* const` is a const pointer to an int (pointer is fixed, data can change).

nodes.title: Pointers and References (3/3)
intro:
**`delete` vs `delete[]`?**

Memory from `new` must be freed with `delete`; memory from `new[]` must be freed with `delete[]` so every element's destructor runs. Mixing them is undefined behavior. Deleting `nullptr` is safe and does nothing.

nodes.title: Types, Initialization & Constants (1/2)
intro:
**Difference between `const` and `constexpr`?**

`const` means read-only after initialization (the value may be determined at runtime). `constexpr` means the value or function can be evaluated at compile time and used in constant expressions.

**What does `auto` deduce, and what are its traps?**

The type of the initializer with top-level `const` and references dropped. `auto x = {1,2,3}` is an `initializer_list`. `auto y = v[0]` copies; use `const auto&`. `decltype(expr)` keeps the exact type.

**`std::vector<int> v{3, 7}` versus `v(3, 7)`?**

Braces prefer the `initializer_list` constructor: two elements, 3 and 7. Parentheses call the (count, value) constructor: three elements, each 7.

nodes.title: Types, Initialization & Constants (2/2)
intro:
**What are the three meanings of `static`?**

A local variable that lives for the whole program and keeps its value between calls; internal linkage for a global (visible only in this `.cpp`); a class member shared by all objects.

**Which C++17 features do you use?**

`std::optional`, `std::variant`, `std::string_view`, structured bindings, `if constexpr`, `if` with initializer, fold expressions and `[[nodiscard]]`: vocabulary types and clearer code.

nodes.title: Casts and Type Conversions (1/2)
intro:
**When would you use `dynamic_cast`?**

For a checked downcast from a polymorphic base to a derived type when you cannot express the need through a virtual function. It returns null (pointers) or throws `bad_cast` (references) on failure. Frequent use suggests a design problem.

**The four named casts?**

`static_cast` for well-defined conversions, `dynamic_cast` for checked downcasts, `const_cast` to add or remove `const` (modifying a truly const object is UB), `reinterpret_cast` to reinterpret bits (rarely correct). Never a C cast: it can silently pick any of them.

**What is wrong with `if (-1 < 1u)`?**

The signed operand is converted to unsigned, becoming a huge value, so the comparison is false. Avoid mixing signed and unsigned; compile with `-Wsign-compare`.

nodes.title: Casts and Type Conversions (2/2)
intro:
**What does a C-style cast `(T)x` do?**

It tries `static_cast`, then `static_cast` plus `const_cast`, then `reinterpret_cast`, and uses the first that compiles. It can silently remove `const` or reinterpret bytes, and it never becomes `dynamic_cast`. Use the named casts so the intent is visible and searchable.

**What is narrowing, and how do braces help?**

A conversion that can lose information, such as double to int or a value that does not fit. With `=` it compiles silently; with braces the compiler must diagnose it, for example `int b{3.7}` is an error.

**How do you reinterpret the bits of a float as an integer safely?**

With `std::memcpy` or `std::bit_cast` (C++20). A `reinterpret_cast` of the pointer and a read through it as another type violates the aliasing rules.

nodes.title: Classes and Objects (1/2)
intro:
**What does `const` after a member function promise?**

That the function does not modify the object: inside it `this` is a `const T*`. Only such functions can be called on a `const` object, so make every getter `const`.

**In what order are objects constructed and destroyed?**

Construction: base class first, then the members in declaration order, then the body of the constructor. Destruction runs in the exact reverse order.

**Why use the member initializer list?**

It initializes members directly instead of default-constructing and then assigning. `const` and reference members can only be set there. Members are initialized in declaration order, whatever order the list is written in.

nodes.title: Classes and Objects (2/2)
intro:
**What is a class invariant?**

A condition that must hold for every valid object, such as "the balance is never negative". Keep the data private and let only the constructors and member functions change it, so the invariant cannot be broken from outside.

**`struct` or `class`?**

Only the default access differs: `struct` is public, `class` is private. Use `struct` for plain data and `class` when there is an invariant to protect.

**What is RAII in one sentence?**

Acquire a resource in the constructor and release it in the destructor, so the resource lives exactly as long as the object and is freed even when the function returns early or throws.

nodes.title: Copy Control and Operators (1/2)
intro:
**What is the Rule of Three / Five / Zero?**

Three: if you define a destructor, copy constructor or copy assignment, define all three. Five: add the move constructor and move assignment. Zero: design classes so none are needed by holding resources in self-managing members like `vector` and `unique_ptr`. Remember that declaring a destructor or a copy operation suppresses the move operations, so moves silently become copies.

**What does `explicit` do on a constructor and on `operator bool`?**

On a constructor it forbids implicit conversions from the argument type (`Feet f = 3.0` fails). On `operator bool` it allows the conversion only in contexts such as `if` and `while`, not in arithmetic. Mark single-argument constructors `explicit` by default.

nodes.title: Copy Control and Operators (2/2)
intro:
**What is copy-and-swap?**

Write the copy constructor and a non-throwing `swap`, then implement `operator=(T other)` by value that swaps with the parameter. The copy happens before `*this` is modified, giving the strong exception guarantee and safe self-assignment with one function.

**Member or non-member operator?**

Operators that change the left operand (`+=`) are members. Operators where both sides should convert (`+`, `==`) are non-members, built from the member ones. `operator<<` for printing must be a non-member because its left operand is the stream.

nodes.title: Inheritance, Virtual Functions and the Object Model (1/3)
intro:
**Why must a base class destructor be virtual?**

If you `delete` a derived object through a base pointer and the destructor is not virtual, only the base destructor runs: undefined behavior, and the derived part's resources leak. A virtual destructor makes `delete` dispatch to the most derived destructor first. Any class meant to be a polymorphic base needs one.

**What is the difference between overloading and overriding?**

Overloading: several functions with the same name and different parameters in the same scope, chosen at compile time. Overriding: a derived class provides its own implementation of a base virtual function with the same signature, chosen at runtime.

**What is a pure virtual function and an abstract class?**

A pure virtual function is declared `= 0` and has no required implementation. A class with at least one cannot be instantiated; it defines an interface that derived classes must implement.

**What is object slicing?**

Copying a derived object into a base-class value discards the derived members and virtual behaviour. Avoid it by passing polymorphic objects by reference or pointer.

nodes.title: Inheritance, Virtual Functions and the Object Model (2/3)
intro:
**Can a constructor be virtual? Can a destructor be pure virtual?**

A constructor cannot be virtual: the vptr is set up by the constructor, so there is no dynamic type yet. A destructor can be pure virtual to make a class abstract, but it still needs a body because derived destructors call it.

**Composition or inheritance?**

Prefer composition. Use public inheritance only for a true is-a relationship where you need runtime polymorphism, and make sure it satisfies Liskov substitution.

**What is the diamond problem and how is it solved?**

A class inherits the same base through two paths, so the base's members are duplicated and access is ambiguous. Virtual inheritance (`class Left : virtual Base`) makes all paths share one base subobject, which the most derived class constructs first. It adds memory and indirection, so prefer interfaces without data or composition.

**Why do `Reader*` and `Writer*` to the same `File` hold different addresses?**

With multiple inheritance the object contains each base subobject at its own offset, each with its own vptr. Converting to the second base adjusts the pointer to that subobject, which is why C casts and `reinterpret_cast` are wrong here.

nodes.title: Inheritance, Virtual Functions and the Object Model (3/3)
intro:
**What does `dynamic_cast` need and what does it cost?**

A polymorphic class (a virtual function) because it reads the type information next to the vtable. It checks the real type at run time: null for pointers, `std::bad_cast` for references. It is slower than a virtual call, so avoid it on hot paths; repeated use suggests a missing virtual function or a Visitor.

**`typeid` on a polymorphic versus non-polymorphic type?**

On a polymorphic object `typeid(*p)` gives the dynamic type. On a type with no virtual function it gives the static type, known at compile time. `type_info::name()` is implementation-defined and only for diagnostics.

**When is private inheritance appropriate?**

For "implemented in terms of": to override a virtual function of the base, access its protected members, or use the empty base optimisation. Otherwise prefer composition. It does not allow conversion to the base outside the class.

nodes.title: Function Pointers and Functors (1/2)
intro:
**What is a function pointer, and what can it not do?**

The address of a function, 8 bytes, callable like the function. It cannot carry state: the function sees only its arguments and globals. The call goes through the pointer, so it is rarely inlined.

**What is a functor?**

A class with an `operator()`. Its objects are called like functions and keep state in their members. Each class is its own type, so templates can inline the call.

**Why can a plain function pointer not carry a "limit" value for a comparison?**

A function pointer is only an address. The function it points to receives its arguments and can read globals, nothing else. A functor or a lambda stores the limit as a member.

nodes.title: Function Pointers and Functors (2/2)
intro:
**`std::function` vs a template parameter?**

A template parameter keeps the exact callable type, so the call is inlined and nothing allocates. `std::function` erases the type: one indirect call, possible allocation, but it can store different callables behind one type.

**How do you call a member function through a pointer?**

With `std::invoke(&Account::balance, acct)`, or `(acct.*pmf)()` for a pointer-to-member `pmf`. `std::invoke` works for every kind of callable.

nodes.title: Lambdas (1/2)
intro:
**What is a lambda and what does the compiler generate?**

An unnamed function object: the compiler creates a unique class with the captured variables as members and the body as `operator()`. Because it has its own type, calls can be inlined.

**Capture by value vs by reference?**

By value copies the variable when the lambda is created (const inside unless `mutable`). By reference stores a reference to the live variable and dangles if the lambda outlives it. Capture by value for lambdas that escape the scope or run on another thread.

**How do you move a `unique_ptr` into a lambda?**

With a C++14 init-capture: `[p = std::move(ptr)] { ... }`. A plain capture would need a copy, which `unique_ptr` forbids.

nodes.title: Lambdas (2/2)
intro:
**What does `mutable` do on a lambda?**

It makes `operator()` non-const so the lambda can modify its by-value captures. The changes live in the lambda's own copy, not in the original variable.

**What is a generic lambda?**

A lambda with `auto` parameters (C++14): its `operator()` is a template, so one lambda works for any argument type.

**What is wrong with capturing `this` by `[=]`?**

`[=]` inside a member function captures the `this` pointer, not a copy of the object, so the lambda dangles if the object is destroyed first. It is deprecated in C++20: write `[=, this]` or `[*this]` to copy.

nodes.title: STL Containers (1/2)
intro:
**How does `std::vector` grow?**

When `size == capacity` it allocates a larger buffer (geometric growth, typically 1.5x to 2x, implementation-defined), moves or copies the elements, and frees the old buffer. This makes `push_back` amortised O(1), but it invalidates all iterators, pointers and references. `reserve` avoids the reallocations.

**`push_back` vs `emplace_back`?**

`push_back` takes an existing object (a copy or move). `emplace_back` forwards its arguments to the element's constructor and builds it in place, avoiding a temporary. For simple types there is no difference; for objects with expensive construction `emplace_back` can save a move.

nodes.title: STL Containers (2/2)
intro:
**Which container for a task queue? For "top K" elements?**

A queue (`std::queue`, backed by `deque`) for FIFO tasks. A `priority_queue` (heap) for top K: keep a heap of size K and compare against its root: O(n log K).

**How do you return several values from a function?**

A `std::pair` or `std::tuple`, unpacked with structured bindings (`auto [a, b] = f();`), or a small named struct when the fields need names or the result travels. Not out-parameters, except where you want to reuse a buffer.

nodes.title: Maps, Sets and Hashing (1/2)
intro:
**How do you use your own type as a key in `unordered_map`, and in `map`?**

`unordered_map`: provide `operator==` and a hash functor (or specialise `std::hash`) that combines all members; equal objects must hash equally. `map`: provide a strict weak ordering (`operator<` or a comparator type). Never `<=`, and never modify a key while it is stored.

**Why use `try_emplace` instead of `emplace` or `insert`?**

If the key exists, `try_emplace` does nothing and does not touch its arguments, so a moved-in value is not lost. `emplace` and `insert` may already have built or moved from the value. It is the right call for "insert if absent" with expensive or move-only values.

**`map` vs `unordered_map`?**

`map`: balanced tree, sorted iteration, O(log n), needs `operator<`, supports range queries. `unordered_map`: hash table, average O(1) (worst O(n) with many collisions), no order, needs a hash and `==`. Choose `unordered_map` for plain lookups and `map` when you need order.

nodes.title: Maps, Sets and Hashing (2/2)
intro:
**What is a hash collision and how is it handled?**

Two different keys hash to the same bucket. The standard library's unordered containers resolve it with chaining (a bucket holds a list of entries), so lookups in a heavily colliding bucket degrade toward O(n). A good hash function and a sensible load factor (`rehash`, `reserve`) keep it near O(1).

**Why does `m[key]` on a missing key matter?**

`operator[]` inserts a default-constructed value and returns a reference to it, so reading a missing key grows the map. To only look, use `find`, `count` or `contains` (C++20); `at()` throws instead of inserting.

**How do you return several values from a function?**

A `std::pair` or `std::tuple` read with structured bindings (`auto [lo, hi] = minmax(v)`) when the values are used right away; a small named `struct` when they travel further and deserve names.

nodes.title: Iterators (1/2)
intro:
**What does `std::back_inserter` do and when do you need it?**

It is an output iterator whose assignment calls `push_back`. Algorithms such as `copy` and `transform` write through iterators and do not grow the destination, so with an empty target you would write past the end; `back_inserter` makes them grow it instead.

**Why can't I `std::sort` a `std::list`?**

`sort` needs random-access iterators (it jumps around by index). A list only provides bidirectional iterators, so it has its own member function `list::sort`.

**What does `std::span` replace, and what is its danger?**

It replaces a `(pointer, count)` pair: a non-owning view of contiguous elements that remembers its size and accepts a vector, an array or a part of either, without copying. Like `string_view` it dangles if the data is destroyed or reallocated while the view is alive.

nodes.title: Iterators (2/2)
intro:
**What is iterator invalidation, and when does `push_back` cause it?**

A change to the container can leave existing iterators, pointers and references pointing at memory that no longer holds the element: using them is undefined behavior. `vector::push_back` invalidates all of them when it reallocates, otherwise only `end()`. Node-based containers (`list`, `map`, `set`) keep them valid except for an erased element.

**Why is a range written `[begin, end)`, and why compare with `!=`?**

`end()` is one past the last element, so an empty range is simply `begin == end` and the length is `end - begin`. Only `!=` works for every container; `<` exists only for random-access iterators.

nodes.title: Algorithms and Ranges (1/2)
intro:
**What are C++20 ranges and views?**

Ranges algorithms take a whole container (`std::ranges::sort(v)`) and support projections. Views are lazy, non-owning pipelines (`v | views::filter(f) | views::transform(g)`) that compute on demand without temporaries. Like `string_view`, a view dangles if its container dies.

**What is the erase-remove idiom?**

`std::remove`/`remove_if` only moves the elements to keep to the front and returns the new end; it cannot shrink the container. Pass that to the container's `erase` to actually delete the tail: `v.erase(std::remove_if(...), v.end())`. C++20 has `std::erase_if`.

**Why must a comparator for `sort` be a strict weak ordering?**

The algorithm assumes that "less" is irreflexive (`comp(a, a)` is false) and transitive. A comparator such as `<=` is true for equal elements, so `sort` can run past the end of the range or crash. Use `<`, and `stable_sort` when equal elements must keep their order.

nodes.title: Algorithms and Ranges (2/2)
intro:
**Why does `lower_bound` need a sorted range?**

It is a binary search: it compares with the middle element and discards half the range each step. That is only correct if the elements are ordered by the same comparison. On unsorted data the answer is meaningless. It is O(log n) on random-access iterators.

**Why use `<random>` instead of `rand() % n`?**

`rand()` has poor quality, global state, and the modulo skews the distribution. An engine (`mt19937`) produces bits and a distribution (`uniform_int_distribution`) shapes them; one engine per thread, seeded from `random_device` or a fixed value for repeatable tests.

nodes.title: Function Templates (1/3)
intro:
**How are template arguments deduced?**

From the arguments of the call, by the shape of the parameter. By value (`T x`): `const` and references are dropped and arrays decay to pointers. By reference (`T& x`): `const` and the array size are kept. `T&&` is a forwarding reference. No conversions take part, so `maxOf(3, 2.5)` fails; name `T` explicitly.

**What happens when you use a function template?**

The compiler deduces the template arguments from the call, then **instantiates** a concrete function for that combination of types (once per distinct combination across the program), and compiles it like normal code. The template itself generates no code.

nodes.title: Function Templates (2/3)
intro:
**What is a forwarding reference?**

A `T&&` parameter where `T` is deduced for that very function template (or `auto&&`). It binds to lvalues and rvalues alike: for an lvalue `T` becomes `X&` and reference collapsing makes the parameter `X&`; for an rvalue `T` is `X` and the parameter is `X&&`. `std::forward` then preserves that category.

**What is a variadic template and how do you process the pack?**

A template taking zero or more arguments via a parameter pack (`typename... Args`). Expand with `args...`. Process by recursion with a base case, or in C++17 with a fold expression like `(args + ...)`.

nodes.title: Function Templates (3/3)
intro:
**Templates vs inheritance for polymorphism?**

Templates give static (compile-time) polymorphism: no runtime cost and inlinable, but the type must be known when compiling and each type duplicates code. Inheritance with virtual functions gives dynamic (runtime) polymorphism: one code path and heterogeneous collections, at the cost of an indirection and heap-allocated objects.

nodes.title: Class Templates (1/2)
intro:
**What are alias templates and variable templates?**

An alias template is a parameterised `using` (`template<class T> using Vec = std::vector<T>;`), which a `typedef` cannot be. A variable template is a constant or variable per type (`template<class T> constexpr T zero = T{};`); `std::is_integral_v` is one.

**Full vs partial specialization?**

Full: all template arguments fixed. Partial: a pattern with some parameters still free (`Foo<T*>`), allowed for class templates and variable templates but not for function templates (use overloading).

**Why must template definitions be in headers?**

The compiler needs the body to instantiate it in each translation unit that uses a particular type. If only the declaration is visible, no instantiation happens and the linker cannot find the function. Alternative: explicit instantiation in one `.cpp`.

nodes.title: Class Templates (2/2)
intro:
**What is a non-type template parameter?**

A template parameter that is a compile-time value instead of a type, such as the `N` in `std::array<int, N>`. Each value gives a different type, which is why `Stack<int, 8>` and `Stack<int, 9>` are unrelated.

**What is class template argument deduction?**

Since C++17 the compiler can deduce the arguments of a class template from the constructor call: `std::vector v{1, 2, 3}` is a `vector<int>`. A deduction guide tells it how when the constructors alone are not enough.

nodes.title: Type Traits, Concepts and Compile-time C++ (1/3)
intro:
**What does SFINAE stand for and why does it exist?**

Substitution Failure Is Not An Error: an invalid substitution while deducing a template removes that candidate from overload resolution instead of causing a hard error. It is what makes `enable_if` overload selection work.

**`std::is_same_v<int, const int>`?**

False. They are different types. `const` and references are part of the type, which is why traits like `std::decay_t` and `std::remove_cvref_t` exist.

nodes.title: Type Traits, Concepts and Compile-time C++ (2/3)
intro:
**`constexpr` function versus `consteval` function?**

`constexpr` may run at compile time or run time. `consteval` must run at compile time and is a compile error otherwise.

**Why is `if constexpr` better than `if` in a template?**

The discarded branch is not instantiated, so code that is invalid for some `T` does not break the build for that `T`.

nodes.title: Type Traits, Concepts and Compile-time C++ (3/3)
intro:
**What is a concept, and why is it better than `enable_if`?**

A concept is a named compile-time condition on template arguments (`std::integral<T>`, or your own with `requires`). It states the interface of a template in the signature and fails at the call site with a readable "constraint not satisfied" message, where `enable_if` gives pages of substitution errors.

**How do you avoid writing the factorial struct by hand today?**

Write `constexpr int factorial(int n)` and use it in a `constexpr` context. It is shorter, readable and can also run at run time.

nodes.title: RAII and Exceptions (1/2)
intro:
**What is RAII and why is it important?**

It binds a resource's lifetime to an object: acquire in the constructor, release in the destructor. Cleanup is automatic and exception-safe because destructors run on every exit path. It replaces `try/finally` and is why C++ needs no garbage collector.

**What is stack unwinding?**

When an exception propagates, the runtime exits scopes up the call stack, calling the destructors of all fully constructed locals until a handler is found. It is what makes RAII exception-safe.

**Why should destructors not throw?**

Destructors run during unwinding. If one throws while another exception is active, `std::terminate` is called. Destructors are `noexcept` by default; catch and handle errors inside them.

**What are the exception-safety guarantees?**

No-throw (never throws: destructors, swap, moves), strong (if it throws, the state is exactly as before: commit or rollback), and basic (nothing leaks and invariants hold, but values may have changed). Get the strong guarantee by doing the work on a copy and publishing with a non-throwing swap.

nodes.title: RAII and Exceptions (2/2)
intro:
**Why mark move operations `noexcept`?**

`std::vector` moves its elements when it grows only if the move cannot throw; otherwise it copies them to keep the strong guarantee. A missing `noexcept` silently turns every reallocation into a round of copies.

**What happens if a `noexcept` function throws?**

`std::terminate` is called: the exception does not propagate. So only promise `noexcept` when it is true.

**How do you run cleanup on every path without `finally`?**

Put it in a destructor: a standard RAII wrapper (`lock_guard`, `unique_ptr`, `fstream`) or a small scope guard class. Release the guard on success to commit.

nodes.title: Writing RAII Wrappers
intro: An RAII wrapper **acquires the resource in its constructor and releases it in its destructor**. Destructors run on every way out of a scope, including an exception, so the resource cannot leak.
Make the wrapper **non-copyable** (or give it real copy semantics) and **movable**. A copy that shares a raw handle would release the same resource twice.

nodes.title: Exception Safety in Practice
intro: Code is exception safe at one of three levels: **basic** (no leaks, objects still valid), **strong** (all or nothing) and **nothrow** (never throws).
The usual route to the strong guarantee: do the risky work on a **copy or a temporary**, then **swap** it in with an operation that cannot throw.

nodes.title: noexcept and Error Handling
intro: `noexcept` is a **promise** that a function does not throw. If one does, `std::terminate` is called. Mark **moves, swap and destructors** `noexcept`: containers use that to stay fast and safe.
Throwing costs **nothing on the happy path** but is slow when it happens, so exceptions are for **rare failures**, not for ordinary control flow.

nodes.title: Values or Errors: optional, variant and expected (1/2)
intro:
**What is a vocabulary type?**

A small standard type that expresses a common idea in a signature: `optional` (maybe a value), `variant` (one of several types), `expected` (a value or an error), `span` and `string_view` (a non-owning view). They replace magic values, tagged unions and pointer-plus-count pairs, so the contract is visible and checked.

**`optional` versus a pointer for "may be absent"?**

`optional<T>` holds the value itself (no heap allocation, no ownership question) and is empty when absent. A pointer means "refers to something owned elsewhere" and can be null. Use `optional` for a possibly missing value, a pointer for a possibly missing reference.

**What happens on `*opt`, `opt.value()` and `opt.value_or(x)` when it is empty?**

`*opt` is undefined behaviour, `value()` throws `std::bad_optional_access`, and `value_or(x)` returns `x`. Test with `if (opt)` first when you can.

**How does `std::variant` differ from a `union`?**

A variant remembers which alternative is active (`index()`), destroys the old one and constructs the new one on assignment, works with non-trivial types such as `std::string`, and throws `bad_variant_access` if you read the wrong one. A raw union does none of that, and reading the wrong member is undefined behaviour.

nodes.title: Values or Errors: optional, variant and expected (2/2)
intro:
**Why is `std::visit` safer than a chain of `if` / `get_if`?**

The visitor must handle every alternative, so adding a type to the variant makes every incomplete visitor a compile error instead of a silent missing case. It also reads the active alternative without a manual check.

**Variant or virtual functions for a set of message or shape types?**

A variant when the set of types is closed and you keep adding operations: values are stored inline, there are no allocations or virtual calls, and the compiler checks completeness. Virtual functions when the set of types is open for others to extend and the operations are few.

**`optional`, `expected`, exception or error code?**

`optional` when "no value" needs no explanation. `expected<T, E>` (C++23) when the failure is normal and the reason matters. An exception for rare failures the local code cannot handle, and for constructors. An error code only at C boundaries.

**Exceptions or error codes?**

Exceptions for rare failures the local code cannot handle (and constructors); return values (`optional`, error codes, `expected`) for expected failures and for hot paths where a throw's cost and unpredictability are unacceptable.

nodes.title: Lvalues and Rvalues (1/2)
intro:
**What are lvalues, prvalues and xvalues?**

An lvalue is a named object with an address. A prvalue is an unnamed temporary (a literal, `a + b`, a call returning by value). An xvalue is an object marked as movable, such as `std::move(x)`. Rvalue means prvalue or xvalue. A named rvalue-reference parameter is still an lvalue inside the function.

**What is the address test for lvalues and rvalues?**

If you can take the address of an expression with `&`, it is an lvalue. A literal, `a + b` or the result of a call that returns by value is an rvalue and has no address.

nodes.title: Lvalues and Rvalues (2/2)
intro:
**Which reference types bind to an rvalue?**

`const T&` and `T&&`. A plain `T&` binds only to lvalues. When both a `const T&` and a `T&&` overload exist, an rvalue chooses `T&&`.

**Inside `void g(std::string&& s)`, is `s` an lvalue or an rvalue?**

An lvalue: it has a name and you can use it more than once. To pass it on as an rvalue you must write `std::move(s)`.

nodes.title: Copy versus Move, and std::move (1/2)
intro:
**What does `std::move` actually do?**

Nothing at runtime: it is an unconditional cast to an rvalue reference. It enables the move constructor or move assignment to be chosen. The moved-from object stays valid but unspecified. On a `const` object it silently copies, because a `const` rvalue cannot bind to a move constructor.

**What state is a moved-from object in?**

Valid but unspecified: you may destroy it or assign a new value to it, but not rely on its contents. For standard types it is usually empty.

**Why does `std::move` on a `const` object copy?**

The cast gives a `const T&&`, which cannot bind to the move constructor's `T&&` parameter, so overload resolution picks the copy constructor. No error, just a copy.

nodes.title: Copy versus Move, and std::move (2/2)
intro:
**When is moving not faster than copying?**

For types that own no resource: an `int` or a small struct is just copied. The gain is for types that own memory, handles or other resources.

**Is it safe to use an object after `std::move`?**

Only to destroy it or assign a new value to it. Its contents are unspecified, so do not read them.

nodes.title: Writing Move Operations (1/2)
intro:
**Why mark a move constructor `noexcept`?**

`std::vector` moves its elements on reallocation only if the move cannot throw; otherwise it copies them to keep the strong guarantee. Without `noexcept` every growth becomes a round of copies.

**What does a move constructor do to the source object?**

It steals the resources (pointers, handles) and resets the source to a safe empty state, for example with `std::exchange(o.p, nullptr)`, so the source destructor frees nothing.

**What is copy-and-swap assignment?**

`T& operator=(T o) { swap(*this, o); return *this; }`: the parameter is copied or moved depending on the argument, then swapped in. The old contents are destroyed with `o`. It handles self-assignment and gives the strong guarantee.

nodes.title: Writing Move Operations (2/2)
intro:
**What does the Rule of Zero say?**

Do not write special member functions when members like `vector`, `string` and `unique_ptr` already manage themselves; the compiler's copy and move are then correct.

**Why can declaring a destructor make moves slower?**

A user-declared destructor stops the compiler generating move operations, so moves silently fall back to the copy operations.

nodes.title: Returning Objects and Copy Elision (1/2)
intro:
**What is copy elision / RVO?**

The compiler constructs a returned object directly in the caller's storage, skipping the copy or move. In C++17 it is guaranteed when returning a temporary (prvalue). NRVO for a named local is allowed but not required. Do not write `return std::move(local)`: it prevents it and costs a move.

**Why is `return std::move(local);` a mistake?**

It turns the returned expression into an xvalue, which blocks NRVO. The compiler then must move the object instead of building it in place: an extra move for nothing.

nodes.title: Returning Objects and Copy Elision (2/2)
intro:
**What changed about elision in C++17?**

Returning a prvalue (a temporary such as `return T();`) is guaranteed to build the object directly in the caller's storage, so the type does not even need a copy or move constructor. Elision of a named local (NRVO) is still optional.

**When is `std::move` on a return correct?**

When you return a member of an object that outlives the call, or a by-value parameter's member: it is not the local being named, so no elision applies and moving avoids a copy.

nodes.title: Sink Parameters and Move Traps (1/2)
intro:
**How do you write a class that stores a string argument efficiently?**

Take the parameter by value and `std::move` it into the member. An lvalue costs one copy plus one move, an rvalue costs one move, and there is a single function to write.

**What is the difference between `push_back` and `emplace_back`?**

`push_back` takes an existing object (copied or moved into the container). `emplace_back` forwards its arguments and constructs the element in place, saving a temporary. Both reallocate the same way.

nodes.title: Sink Parameters and Move Traps (2/2)
intro:
**When should a sink parameter not be taken by value?**

For setters and other functions that assign into an existing object: assignment can reuse existing storage, while a by-value parameter always constructs a new object first. Also when the type is expensive to move, where two overloads are better.

**List three traps that make a move silently a copy.**

`std::move` on a `const` object, a type without move operations (or whose moves were suppressed by a user-declared destructor), and a forwarding reference passed on with `std::move` or without `std::forward`.

nodes.title: Perfect Forwarding (1/2)
intro:
**What is perfect forwarding, and why do we need it?**

Passing arguments through a wrapper to another function without changing their value category or constness, so the callee can still choose copy vs move correctly. Without it you would need an overload per combination of lvalue/rvalue/const for every parameter.

**What is the difference between `std::move` and `std::forward`?**

`std::move` always casts to an rvalue. `std::forward<T>` casts to an rvalue only if the argument that was passed was an rvalue, and keeps an lvalue otherwise. Use `forward` only on a forwarding reference, once.

nodes.title: Perfect Forwarding (2/2)
intro:
**What is reference collapsing?**

The rule that resolves a reference to a reference created by templates: `T& &&`, `T&& &` and `T& &` all become `T&`; only `T&& &&` stays `T&&`. It is why a forwarding reference can bind to both lvalues and rvalues.

**Is every `T&&` a forwarding reference?**

No. It must be `T&&` where `T` is deduced for that very function template (or `auto&&`). `std::vector<T>&&`, a `const T&&` and the `T&&` of a class template's member function are plain rvalue references.

nodes.title: unique_ptr: Exclusive Ownership (1/2)
intro:
**What does `unique_ptr` guarantee?**

Exactly one owner at a time. When the owner is destroyed it deletes the object, so you cannot forget to free it or free it twice by accident.

**Why can a `unique_ptr` not be copied?**

Two owners would delete the object twice. Ownership is transferred by moving instead, which leaves the source null.

**How do you pass and return a `unique_ptr`?**

Return it by value from a factory (it moves out). Take it by value, with `std::move` at the call, to take ownership. If the function only uses the object, take `const T&` or `T*` instead.

nodes.title: unique_ptr: Exclusive Ownership (2/2)
intro:
**What is the overhead of `unique_ptr`?**

None with the default deleter: the same size as a raw pointer and the same cost to use. A function-pointer deleter doubles the size; a stateless lambda adds nothing.

**`get()`, `release()` and `reset()`?**

`get()` returns the raw pointer and keeps ownership. `release()` gives up ownership and returns the pointer, so you must delete it. `reset()` destroys the object now.

nodes.title: shared_ptr: Shared Ownership (1/2)
intro:
**`unique_ptr` vs `shared_ptr` vs `weak_ptr`?**

`unique_ptr`: sole owner, move-only, zero overhead. `shared_ptr`: reference-counted shared ownership with a control block and atomic count. `weak_ptr`: non-owning observer used to break cycles and to check whether a shared object is still alive (`lock()`).

**Is `shared_ptr` thread-safe?**

The reference count is atomic, so copying and destroying `shared_ptr`s from different threads is safe. The pointed-to object is **not** protected: concurrent access to it still needs synchronization. Concurrently modifying the same `shared_ptr` variable is also a race.

**Why prefer `make_unique` / `make_shared`?**

No naked `new`, less typing (and exception safe before C++17), and `make_shared` allocates the object and its control block once instead of twice.

nodes.title: shared_ptr: Shared Ownership (2/2)
intro:
**How do you pass a smart pointer to a function?**

If the function only uses the object, pass a reference or raw pointer, not the smart pointer. To transfer ownership, take a `unique_ptr` by value and have the caller `std::move`. To share, take a `shared_ptr` by value. Return `unique_ptr` from factories.

**Why can two `shared_ptr`s built from the same raw pointer crash?**

Each creates its own control block and count, so the object is deleted twice. Copy an existing `shared_ptr`, or inherit `enable_shared_from_this` when an object must hand out a shared pointer to itself.

**Does `unique_ptr` cost anything compared with a raw pointer?**

Not with the default deleter: it is the same size and the destructor inlines to a `delete`. A stateful deleter (a capturing lambda, a function pointer) makes it larger.

nodes.title: weak_ptr and Reference Cycles (1/2)
intro:
**How do you break a `shared_ptr` cycle?**

Make one direction (usually the child's link to its parent) a `weak_ptr`. It does not count toward ownership, so the objects can be destroyed; use `lock()` to get a temporary `shared_ptr` when needed.

**Why must you call `lock()` instead of checking `expired()` first?**

Another thread can release the last owner between the check and the use. `lock()` atomically gives you an owner or an empty pointer, so test that result and use it.

**What does a `weak_ptr` keep alive?**

Only the control block (the counts), never the object. That is what lets `expired()` answer after the object is gone.

nodes.title: weak_ptr and Reference Cycles (2/2)
intro:
**Why does `make_shared` delay freeing memory when a `weak_ptr` remains?**

The object and the control block share one allocation. The object is destroyed on time, but the block of memory is released only when the last weak reference goes.

**Name three uses of `weak_ptr`.**

Parent back links in a tree, caches that must not keep unused entries alive, and observer lists that must not keep listeners alive.

nodes.title: Threads: The Mental Model and Your First Thread (1/2)
intro:
**What is the difference between a process and a thread?**

A process has its own address space; threads of one process share memory but each has its own stack and registers. Thread creation and switching are cheaper, communication is easy (shared memory) but needs synchronization.

**What happens if a `std::thread` is destroyed while still joinable, and why?**

`std::terminate` is called. The alternatives are worse: an implicit `join` can hide long waits, and an implicit `detach` leaves a running thread using locals that may be gone (undefined behavior). So make the thread unjoinable on every path: join in an RAII guard, or use `std::jthread` (C++20), which joins automatically.

nodes.title: Threads: The Mental Model and Your First Thread (2/2)
intro:
**What happens if a `std::thread` is destroyed while still joinable, and why?**

`std::terminate` is called. The alternatives are worse: an implicit `join` can hide long waits, and an implicit `detach` leaves a running thread using locals that may be gone (undefined behavior). So make the thread unjoinable on every path: join in an RAII guard, or use `std::jthread` (C++20), which joins automatically.

nodes.title: Shared Data and Data Races (1/2)
intro:
**What is a data race? Is it the same as a race condition?**

A data race is unsynchronised concurrent access to the same memory with at least one write: undefined behavior in C++. A race condition is the wider class of bugs where correctness depends on timing, which can exist even without a data race (two correctly locked steps that needed to be one atomic operation).

**Is a function-local `static` initialised thread-safely?**

Yes, since C++11 initialization happens exactly once even with concurrent callers ("magic statics"). That is why the Meyers Singleton is thread-safe. Using the object afterwards still needs its own synchronization.

nodes.title: Shared Data and Data Races (2/2)
intro:
**Why is `++counter` not safe on two threads?**

It is three steps: load, add, store. If both threads load before either stores, one increment is lost. Use a mutex or `std::atomic`.

**What are the three ways to share data safely?**

Do not share (each thread owns its data and results are merged), share but never modify (`const` data), or share and protect with a mutex or an atomic.

nodes.title: Mutexes and Locking (1/2)
intro:
**`lock_guard` vs `unique_lock` vs `scoped_lock`?**

`lock_guard`: simplest RAII lock for a scope. `unique_lock`: flexible (unlock/relock, deferred, movable) and needed by condition variables. `scoped_lock` (C++17): locks multiple mutexes at once with deadlock avoidance.

**My class locks a mutex in every method. Is it thread-safe?**

Not necessarily. Each call is safe on its own, but a caller's sequence of calls is not atomic. The classic case is a shared stack: `if (!s.empty()) { v = s.top(); s.pop(); }` races, because another thread can pop between the check and the use. The cause is the interface (it is also true of a lock-free stack), so the fix is to provide whole operations such as `std::optional<T> try_pop()` that check and remove under one lock.

nodes.title: Mutexes and Locking (2/2)
intro:
**What does `std::scoped_lock` do?**

It locks several mutexes in one step with a deadlock-avoidance algorithm and unlocks them in its destructor. Use it whenever you need more than one lock.

**When would you use `std::shared_mutex`?**

For read-mostly data: many readers take a `shared_lock` at the same time, a writer takes a `unique_lock` and excludes everyone. It only pays when reads greatly outnumber writes.

nodes.title: Deadlock (1/2)
intro:
**What is a deadlock and how do you prevent it?**

Threads wait for each other's locks forever. Needs mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption and circular wait. Prevent with a consistent global lock order, `std::scoped_lock`/`std::lock` for multiple mutexes, short critical sections, no calls to foreign code under a lock, or `try_lock`.

**Can threads deadlock without any mutex? What are the practical rules against deadlock?**

Yes: two threads that `join()` each other, or any cycle of waits on futures or condition variables. The rules all mean "do not wait for a thread that might be waiting for you": avoid nested locks (or take several with `scoped_lock`), never call user-supplied code or leak references to protected data while holding a lock, lock in a fixed order, and use a lock hierarchy so a wrong order is caught immediately at runtime.

nodes.title: Deadlock (2/2)
intro:
**What are the four Coffman conditions?**

Mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption and circular wait. All four must hold for a deadlock; breaking any one prevents it. A global lock order breaks circular wait.

**Why is `std::scoped_lock(a, b)` safe when two threads pass the mutexes in opposite orders?**

It takes the locks with a deadlock-avoidance algorithm (try-and-back-off or ordering), so the order of the arguments does not matter.

nodes.title: Condition Variables and Debugging (1/2)
intro:
**Why does `condition_variable::wait` need a predicate / a loop?**

Spurious wakeups (a thread may wake without a notification) and because the state may change again between the notification and the thread reacquiring the lock. The predicate re-checks the real condition.

**Why must the shared condition be modified under the mutex?**

Otherwise the waiter could check the condition (false), then the notifier changes it and notifies, then the waiter goes to sleep: a lost wakeup. The mutex makes check-and-sleep atomic with respect to the update.

**How would you find a data race in a large program?**

Build and run the tests with ThreadSanitizer (`-fsanitize=thread`), and Helgrind for lock-order problems; review shared state and make sure every access has a lock or is atomic; reduce sharing by design.

nodes.title: Condition Variables and Debugging (2/2)
intro:
**What is a spurious wakeup?**

A waiting thread can return from `wait` without anyone having notified it. That is why the wait is always paired with a predicate that is re-checked after each wakeup.

**What does `wait` do with the mutex?**

It must be given a `unique_lock`. `wait` unlocks it while the thread sleeps and locks it again before returning, so the predicate is always checked under the lock.

nodes.title: Futures, async and Promises (1/2)
intro:
**`std::async` vs `std::thread`?**

`async` returns a `future` carrying the result and any exception, and may use a pool or defer execution (use `launch::async` to force a thread). `thread` gives raw control with no result channel. A future from `async` blocks in its destructor.

**What are `promise`, `future` and `packaged_task`?**

A `promise` is the write end of a one-shot channel, a `future` the read end. A `packaged_task` wraps a callable and fulfils a future with its result or exception, which is how a pool returns results. A `shared_future` is a copyable read end for several waiters.

**How would you signal several threads to start at the same moment?**

A `promise<void>` whose `shared_future` every thread waits on, or a `std::latch`/`barrier`. The promise is one-shot; for repeated signals use a condition variable.

nodes.title: Futures, async and Promises (2/2)
intro:
**Why does a discarded `std::async` future make the call synchronous?**

The future returned by `async` waits for its task in its destructor. A temporary is destroyed at the end of the statement, so the statement blocks until the task has finished.

**How does an exception from a task reach the caller?**

It is caught inside the task, stored in the shared state, and rethrown by `future::get()`.

nodes.title: Thread Pools, Coordination and Parallel Algorithms (1/2)
intro:
**How would you signal several threads to start at the same moment?**

A `promise<void>` whose `shared_future` every thread waits on, or a `std::latch`/`barrier`. The promise is one-shot; for repeated signals use a condition variable.

**Why is the task run outside the lock in a thread-pool worker?**

Otherwise only one task could run at a time, and the queue would stay locked while a task works. The worker takes the task under the lock, releases it, then runs the task.

**How many threads should a pool have?**

About `hardware_concurrency()` for CPU-bound work (more means oversubscription and context switches), more for I/O-bound or blocking work. Use separate pools for mixed workloads.

**What is work stealing?**

Each worker has its own deque of tasks and pops from it; an idle worker steals from the back of another's deque. Owners and thieves work at opposite ends, so contention is low and load balances automatically. It removes the single shared queue's lock as a bottleneck.

nodes.title: Thread Pools, Coordination and Parallel Algorithms (2/2)
intro:
**What is the difference between `latch` and `barrier`?**

A `latch` is a one-shot countdown: threads count down and others wait until it reaches zero. A `barrier` is reusable: a fixed group of threads waits for each other at the end of each phase, then all continue together.

**What does a semaphore do that a mutex does not?**

A counting semaphore allows up to k threads in at once (a permit counter) and can be released by a different thread than the one that acquired it. A mutex is one owner at a time and must be unlocked by its owner.

**How do you stop a thread cleanly?**

Cooperatively: ask it to stop and let it return. C++20 `std::jthread` passes a `std::stop_token` that the loop checks, and its destructor requests the stop and joins. There is no safe forced kill.

**When is a parallel algorithm worth using, and what must you watch?**

For large inputs and non-trivial work per element. The callback must be thread-safe, `reduce` needs an associative operation, and small ranges are slower because of thread overhead. Without a parallel backend the call runs serially.

nodes.title: Atomics and Compare-and-Swap (1/2)
intro:
**`std::atomic` vs mutex?**

An atomic makes operations on a single variable indivisible, usually lock-free and cheap. A mutex protects any critical section, including invariants over several variables, but may block. Use atomics for counters and flags, mutexes for compound state.

**Is `volatile` a substitute for `atomic`?**

No. `volatile` prevents some compiler optimisations but gives no atomicity and no inter-thread ordering. Using it for synchronization is a data race.

**`compare_exchange_weak` vs `strong`?**

Both set a value only if it still equals the expected one. `weak` may fail spuriously, so it belongs in a retry loop and is cheaper on some CPUs; `strong` fails only on a real mismatch and suits a single attempt. On failure they load the current value into `expected`.

nodes.title: Atomics and Compare-and-Swap (2/2)
intro:
**What is the ABA problem?**

A CAS succeeds because the value is A again, but it went A to B to A in between, and the structure around it changed (for example a node was freed and reused). Fix with a version counter beside the pointer, or hazard pointers or epoch reclamation.

**When is a spinlock appropriate?**

For very short critical sections on dedicated cores where waiting is shorter than a context switch. It burns CPU while waiting and is dangerous if the holder can be descheduled. Otherwise use a mutex.

nodes.title: The Memory Model: Orders and Happens-Before (1/3)
intro:
**What are the memory orders?**

`seq_cst` (default, strongest, one global order), `acquire`/`release` (pair a release store with an acquire load to publish data), `acq_rel` for read-modify-write, and `relaxed` (atomicity only). Start with the default; weaken only with a reason and a clear happens-before argument.

**What does release/acquire guarantee?**

Everything the producer wrote before a release store is visible to a thread that reads the stored value with an acquire load. The pair synchronizes-with, which gives a happens-before edge, so the earlier plain writes are not a data race.

**What does happens-before mean?**

If A happens-before B, then A's effects are visible to B. Within a thread it is program order; between threads it exists only through synchronization: atomics with matching orders, mutex unlock/lock, thread start and join, futures. Two conflicting accesses without a happens-before relation are a data race.

nodes.title: The Memory Model: Orders and Happens-Before (2/3)
intro:
**When is `relaxed` enough?**

When no other data depends on the atomic: a statistics counter, an id generator, a shutdown flag that carries no data. The final value is correct, but it orders nothing else.

**Why can code with a wrong memory order work on x86 and fail on ARM?**

x86's hardware already orders ordinary loads and stores like release/acquire, so missing orderings are hidden. ARM and POWER reorder far more, so the same code can read stale data there. The C++ model, not the PC you tested on, defines correctness.

nodes.title: The Memory Model: Orders and Happens-Before (3/3)
intro:
**How is a reference count made thread-safe, and with which orders?**

With an atomic counter: increments can be relaxed, the decrement is `acq_rel` so the thread that drops it to zero sees all other threads' writes before it destroys the object. `shared_ptr`'s control block works this way.

**Mutex, fine-grained locks or lock-free: how do you choose?**

Start with one mutex and measure. Split locks if contention shows up and the structure has independent parts (head and tail of a queue, buckets of a table). Go lock-free only for a proven bottleneck and with a known-correct design, because memory reclamation and ABA make it hard; an SPSC ring buffer is the one case simple enough to write confidently.

nodes.title: Strings, Regex & Time (1/3)
intro:
**When is a `string_view` dangerous?**

When it outlives the string it views: views of temporaries, of locals returned from a function, or of a string that is later modified or reallocated.

**`regex_match` versus `regex_search`?**

`regex_match` must match the whole input. `regex_search` finds a match anywhere inside it.

**How do you iterate over every match?**

`std::sregex_iterator` (or `std::cregex_iterator` for C strings) over the range, compared with a default-constructed end iterator.

**Which clock for a timeout, and why?**

`steady_clock`, because it is monotonic and unaffected by changes to the system time.

nodes.title: Strings, Regex & Time (2/3)
intro:
**Why can `seconds = milliseconds` not compile but `milliseconds = seconds` can?**

Converting to a coarser unit would truncate, so it requires an explicit `duration_cast`. Converting to a finer unit is lossless, so it is implicit.

**What is the small string optimisation?**

Short strings (about 15 characters in libstdc++) are stored inside the `std::string` object, so no heap allocation happens and copying is cheap. Longer strings keep a pointer to a heap block. `reserve` avoids repeated reallocations when you know the size.

**`from_chars` versus `stoi`?**

`from_chars` (C++17) returns an error code, never throws, never allocates and ignores the locale, so it suits hot paths and feed parsing; check that the end pointer reached the end of the token. `stoi` throws `invalid_argument` or `out_of_range` and is for ordinary code.

nodes.title: Strings, Regex & Time (3/3)
intro:
**`std::format` versus streams versus `printf`?**

`std::format` (C++20) is type-safe, stateless and readable. Streams are extensible but keep state (`std::hex` sticks) and are verbose. `printf` has no type checking, so a wrong specifier is undefined behaviour.

**Why is `while (!f.eof())` the wrong way to read a file?**

`eof` becomes true only after a read has failed, so the loop body runs once more with a failed read. Loop on the read itself: `while (std::getline(f, line))`.

**Output: what does this print? `std::string s = "abc"; std::cout << s.find('z') == std::string::npos;`**

It does not compile as intended: `<<` binds tighter than `==`, so it tries to compare the stream with `npos`. Parenthesise: `std::cout << (s.find('z') == std::string::npos);` prints 1.

questions.prompt: What does `std::cout << 7 / 2 << " " << 7 / 2.0;` print?
questions.explanation: Both operands are int in the first expression so integer division truncates to 3. In the second, a double operand makes it floating point: 3.5.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
options: Compile error
questions.explanation: Arguments are passed by value by default, so `f` modified its own copy. Use `int& n` to modify the caller's variable.

questions.prompt: What does `std::cout << (-1 < 1u);` print?
options: 1 (true)
0 (false)
Compile error
Undefined behavior
questions.explanation: Comparing signed and unsigned converts the signed value to unsigned: -1 becomes 4294967295, which is not less than 1. Hence 0.

questions.prompt: The linker prints "undefined reference to `foo(int)`". What does that mean?
options: A syntax error somewhere in the source file that stopped the build early
A function was declared and called, but no definition was linked in
The same function was defined twice, in two different object files, so the symbol clashes
A header file could not be found by the preprocessor, so the call has no declaration
questions.explanation: Compile errors come from the compiler about one file. "Undefined reference" comes from the linker: it could not find the body of a declared function in any object file or library.

questions.prompt: Which line is rejected by the compiler?
options: Line (1), because braces need a type name before the value
Line (2): braces forbid narrowing a double to an int
Line (3): a double cannot initialise an int with =
None: all three compile, though (2) and (3) drop the .7
questions.explanation: Brace initialization rejects narrowing (double to int). The `=` form silently truncates 3.7 to 3 (a common source of bugs, which is why braces are preferred).

questions.prompt: A function needs to read a run of ints. What is the safest way to pass it?
options: A pointer and a separate count: `void f(const int* p, int n)`
A `std::span<const int>`, or a `const std::vector<int>&`
A pointer only, and the function finds the end itself
A global array
questions.explanation: A pointer does not know how many elements it points to, and a (pointer, count) pair lets the two disagree. A span (C++20) or a container reference carries the size with the data and accepts arrays and vectors without copying.

questions.prompt: When should a function take a pointer parameter instead of a reference?
options: When speed matters, since pointers are cheaper to pass than references
When nullptr is a valid argument, which the function must then test for
Whenever the object is large and copying it would be costly for the caller
When the object is const, since a const reference cannot be null
questions.explanation: A reference must refer to a real object, so callers can rely on it. Use a pointer only when passing nothing is meaningful. Prefer a value for tiny types and a (const) reference otherwise.

questions.prompt: A program compiles without errors but the build stops with "undefined reference to `helper()`". Which stage failed?
options: The preprocessor, which could not find a header
The compiler, which rejected the syntax of a line
The linker, which found no definition of `helper()`
The loader, which failed as the program started
questions.explanation: Each .cpp file is compiled on its own. An "undefined reference" comes from the linker: it joined the object files and found a function that was declared but never defined.

questions.prompt: What does `#include <vector>` do?
options: Links the standard vector library into the finished program
Pastes the header text into the file before it is compiled
Downloads the vector code from the internet when the program runs
Tells the linker which vector functions it should keep
questions.explanation: `#include` is handled by the preprocessor: it copies the text of the header into the file. Linking is a later and separate step.

questions.prompt: What does `int n;` hold when it is declared inside a function?
options: Zero, because C++ always zero-initializes variables
An indeterminate value: reading it is undefined behavior
The value left by the previous variable, which is guaranteed to be valid
Nothing: the program does not compile until you initialize it
questions.explanation: Local variables of built-in types are not initialized. Reading one before assigning it is undefined behavior; write `int n{};` or `int n = 0;`.

questions.prompt: What does `7 / 2` evaluate to when both operands are `int`?
options: It does not compile
questions.explanation: Division of two ints is integer division: the fractional part is dropped. Use `7.0 / 2` for 3.5.

questions.prompt: A function only reads a large `std::string` argument. How should it take the parameter?
options: By value, so the caller cannot be affected
By `const` reference, which avoids the copy
By non-const reference, which is the fastest
By pointer, which is the only way to avoid a copy
questions.explanation: A `const` reference avoids copying the string and promises not to modify it. A by-value parameter copies; a non-const reference allows changes the caller did not expect.

questions.prompt: Which tool reports an out-of-bounds write only when your test actually executes that line?
options: clang-tidy, which analyzes the source without running it
AddressSanitizer, which instruments the running program
The preprocessor, which only expands macros and includes
The linker, which only resolves the names between files
questions.explanation: A sanitizer checks the program while it runs, so it sees only the paths your tests take. A static analyzer reads the source without running it.

questions.prompt: What is the value of `x` after this code runs?
options: The address of x
Undefined behavior
questions.explanation: `p` holds the address of `x`, so `*p = 9` writes 9 into `x` itself.

questions.prompt: What does the expression `&x` give you?
options: The value stored in x
The address of x
A reference to the type of x
A copy of x
questions.explanation: Unary `&` is the address-of operator. Do not confuse it with `int&`, where `&` is part of a reference type.

questions.prompt: Which statement does NOT compile?
options: (3) int c = *p;
All three compile
questions.explanation: `const int*` is a pointer to const int: the data cannot be modified through it, but the pointer itself can be re-pointed and the data can be read.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
options: It does not compile
Undefined behavior
questions.explanation: A reference can never be re-bound. `r = b` assigns the value of `b` into the variable `r` aliases, so `a` becomes 2.

questions.prompt: Which of these is true of a C++ reference but NOT of a pointer?
options: It can be re-seated to another object after it is created
It can be left uninitialized and assigned later
It must be bound when declared and can never be null
It can only refer to objects that live on the stack
questions.explanation: References are permanent aliases that must be bound to a real object at declaration. Pointers can be null, uninitialized, or re-pointed.

questions.prompt: In `int* p = new int(5);` where do `p` and the int it points to live?
options: Both live on the stack, because the declaration is inside a function
Both live on the heap, because new was used
p is on the stack; the int it points to is on the heap
p is on the heap; the int is on the stack, since it is a small value
questions.explanation: `p` is an ordinary local variable (stack). `new` allocates the int on the heap. When `f` returns, `p` disappears but the heap int leaks unless you `delete` it first.

questions.prompt: What is wrong with this code?
questions.code:
int* a = new int[10];
delete a;
options: It is fine: delete frees arrays too, though element destructors may not run
It needs delete[] a: new[] and delete must match (undefined behavior)
It leaks only the first element, but the program is otherwise valid
new int[10] is invalid: arrays cannot be heap-allocated
questions.explanation: Memory from `new[]` must be released with `delete[]`. Using plain `delete` is undefined behavior.

questions.prompt: What happens on the last line?
options: Prints the old value 1, because the memory is still intact
Prints 0, because delete zeroes the memory it frees
A compile error, because p is used after the delete
Undefined behavior: p dangles after the delete
questions.explanation: After `delete p`, the pointer still holds the old address but the memory is no longer yours. Reading it is use-after-free: undefined behavior.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
options: The address of the third element
questions.explanation: Pointer arithmetic moves in whole elements. `p + 2` points at `a[2]`, which holds 30. `*(p + 2)` is the same as `p[2]`.

questions.prompt: Inside this function, what does `sizeof(arr)` give?
options: 40, the size of the whole array of 10 ints
10, the number of elements declared in the parameter
8 on a 64-bit machine: the parameter is really a pointer
A compile error, because sizeof cannot take a parameter
questions.explanation: A C array parameter silently decays to a pointer, so the size information is lost. This is a key reason to prefer `std::array` and `std::vector`.

questions.prompt: Which function is safe?
options: Only f
Only g
f and h
All of them
questions.explanation: `f` returns a reference and `h` a pointer to a local that is destroyed when the function returns (dangling). `g` returns a copy of the value, which is fine.

questions.prompt: Why is `nullptr` preferred over `NULL`?
options: It runs faster at run time, because it avoids a comparison with zero in conditions
It has its own type, so it is never taken for the integer 0 in overloads
NULL was removed from the language in C++11, so old code no longer compiles
It can be dereferenced safely, which is why NULL should be avoided in new code
questions.explanation: `NULL` is just 0, so `f(NULL)` may pick `f(int)` over `f(char*)`. `nullptr` converts only to pointer types. Dereferencing either is undefined behavior.

questions.prompt: What best describes `int* const p = &x;`?
options: A pointer to a const int: the int is fixed, but the pointer itself can move on
A const pointer to an int: the pointer is fixed, the int can change
A const pointer to a const int: neither the pointer nor the int can change
A reference to x, written with pointer syntax and bound to x for life
questions.explanation: Read right to left: "p is a const pointer to int". The star separates the pointer (right side) from the data (left side).

questions.prompt: In modern C++, what is the preferred way to hold a dynamically sized array of ints?
options: `int* a = new int[n];`
`int a[n];` on the stack
`std::vector<int>`
`malloc(n * sizeof(int))`
questions.explanation: `std::vector` owns its memory, frees it automatically, grows on demand and offers bounds-checked access via `.at()`. Raw `new[]` and `malloc` leave all that to you.

questions.prompt: Besides allocating memory, what does `new` do that `malloc` does not?
options: It is just a type-safe spelling of malloc with a cast hidden inside
It calls the constructor and returns a typed pointer
It zero-fills the memory before returning it
It places the object on the stack for faster access
questions.explanation: `new` allocates, then constructs the object, and throws `std::bad_alloc` on failure. `malloc` returns raw uninitialized bytes (`void*`) and returns null on failure.

questions.prompt: What is the address of a variable?
options: The value that is stored in the variable right now
The number of the memory box where the variable starts
The number of bytes that the variable uses in memory
The name that the compiler gives to the variable
questions.explanation: Memory is a row of numbered boxes (bytes). A variable's address is the number of the first box it occupies; `&x` gives it.

questions.prompt: With `int* p = a;` pointing at the first element of an int array, how many bytes does `p + 1` move on a typical machine?
options: 1 byte
4 bytes: one int
8 bytes: one pointer
It depends on the address of p
questions.explanation: Pointer arithmetic moves by whole elements, so adding 1 to an `int*` adds `sizeof(int)`, which is 4 bytes on most machines.

questions.prompt: What does this code do? `int* p = new int(1); p = new int(2); delete p;`
options: Frees both ints
Leaks the first int and frees the second
Frees the first int and leaks the second
Causes a double delete
questions.explanation: The second `new` overwrites the only pointer to the first block, so it can never be freed. `delete p` frees the second block.

questions.prompt: What does `auto x = {1, 2, 3};` deduce?
options: std::vector<int>, because braces build a vector
int[3], a built-in array of three ints
std::initializer_list<int>, not a vector
A compile error, since auto cannot take a braced list
questions.explanation: A braced list with `auto =` deduces `std::initializer_list`. It is a famous gotcha: write the type explicitly if you want a vector.

questions.prompt: What is the problem with `for (auto [key, value] : myMap)` for a `std::map<std::string, BigObject>`?
options: It does not compile, because structured bindings need a const map
It copies each pair every iteration; use const auto& instead
It modifies the map's keys while iterating over them
It skips the first element of the map
questions.explanation: `auto` deduces a value type, so each element is copied. Write `for (const auto& [key, value] : myMap)`.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between `const` and `constexpr`?
options: They are the same keyword, spelled differently in C++11 and later
constexpr can be evaluated at compile time; const is only read-only
const is for functions only, constexpr is for variables only
constexpr values always live on the heap, so they are slower to read
questions.explanation: A `const int` may be initialized at runtime. A `constexpr` variable must be a compile-time constant, usable in template arguments and array sizes.

questions.prompt: Which of these was introduced in C++17?
options: Move semantics and rvalue references
std::optional and structured bindings
Lambda expressions and generic auto parameters
Concepts, ranges and coroutines together
questions.explanation: Move semantics, lambdas and smart pointers came in C++11; `optional`, `variant`, `string_view`, structured bindings and `if constexpr` in C++17; concepts and ranges in C++20.

questions.prompt: What are the three meanings of `static` in C++?
options: Constant, shared and fast, depending on where the keyword is written
A persistent local, internal linkage at file scope, a class-level member
Heap allocation, stack allocation and global storage, depending on the context
A synonym for volatile, a synonym for const, and a synonym for global
questions.explanation: Inside a function it persists across calls; at namespace scope it hides the name in the translation unit; on a class member it is shared by all instances.

questions.prompt: What does `int a; std::cout << a;` do inside a function?
options: Prints 0, since locals start zeroed
Prints some leftover value, but the program is still valid
Undefined behavior: reading an uninitialized local
Does not compile, because a has no initializer
questions.explanation: A default-initialized local `int` has an indeterminate value; reading it is undefined behaviour. Initialize with `int a{};` or a value.

questions.prompt: How many elements does `std::vector<int> v{3, 7};` contain?
options: 3 elements, each 7
2 elements: 3 and 7
7 elements
It does not compile
questions.explanation: Braces prefer the `initializer_list` constructor. `std::vector<int> v(3, 7)` with parentheses gives three 7s.

questions.prompt: What happens with `int x{3.7};`?
options: x is 3, truncated just as a C-style cast would do it
x is 4, because the value is rounded to the nearest int
Compile error: narrowing conversion inside braces
Undefined behavior at run time, because 3.7 does not fit
questions.explanation: List-initialization rejects narrowing conversions. `int x = 3.7;` would compile and silently truncate.

questions.prompt: Given `const int ci = 9;`, what are the types of `auto a = ci;` and `decltype(ci) b = 10;`?
options: `int` and `const int`
both `const int`
both `int`
`const int` and `int`
questions.explanation: `auto` drops top-level `const` and references; `decltype` reports the declared type exactly.

questions.prompt: Which of these needs C++20?
options: `std::optional`
Structured bindings
Concepts
`std::string_view`
questions.explanation: `optional`, structured bindings and `string_view` arrived in C++17. Concepts, ranges, `std::span`, coroutines and `operator<=>` are C++20.

questions.prompt: Which declaration leaves a local variable with an undefined value?
options: int a{};
int a = 0;
int a;
int a{0};
questions.explanation: A local variable of a built-in type with no initializer is not set to zero: its value is indeterminate, and reading it is undefined behavior. The other three give it a value.

questions.prompt: Given `const int& r = x;`, what is the type of `auto a = r;`?
options: const int&
const int
int&
int
questions.explanation: `auto` drops top-level const and references, so `a` is a plain `int` holding a copy. Write `const auto&` to keep a reference.

questions.prompt: Which line is a compile-time constant that can be used as an array size?
options: const int n = std::rand();
int n = 4;
constexpr int n = 4;
static int n = std::rand();
questions.explanation: `constexpr` requires a value the compiler can compute. A `const` initialized at run time, or a plain variable, cannot size an array.

questions.prompt: What does `dynamic_cast<Dog*>(animalPtr)` return when the object is not a Dog?
options: The same pointer
nullptr
It throws std::bad_cast
Undefined behavior
questions.explanation: The pointer form returns null on failure; the reference form throws `std::bad_cast`. It requires the base class to be polymorphic (have a virtual function).

questions.prompt: Which cast is the most dangerous and rarely correct?
options: static_cast
dynamic_cast
reinterpret_cast
They are equally safe
questions.explanation: `reinterpret_cast` reinterprets raw bits between unrelated types and bypasses the type system. Prefer `static_cast`, and avoid C-style casts, which can silently act as any of them.

questions.prompt: What is the value of `-1 < 1u`?
options: `true`
`false`
Compile error
Undefined
questions.explanation: The signed -1 is converted to unsigned, becoming a huge number, so the comparison is false. This is why `-Wsign-compare` exists.

questions.prompt: For `std::uint8_t a = 200, b = 100;`, what is the type and value of `a + b`?
options: `uint8_t`, 44
`uint8_t`, runtime error
`unsigned`, 300
questions.explanation: Types smaller than `int` are promoted to `int` before arithmetic, so the sum is 300. Only storing it back into a `uint8_t` wraps it to 44.

questions.prompt: What is `static_cast<int>(-3.9)`?
questions.explanation: Converting a floating-point value to an integer truncates toward zero.

questions.prompt: What does `7 / 2` give when both operands are `int`, and how do you get 3.5?
options: 3, and `7 / 2.0` gives 3.5
3.5, because C++ promotes the result
4, because it rounds
A compile error without a cast
questions.explanation: Integer division drops the fraction. Making one operand a floating-point type, for example `static_cast<double>(7) / 2` or `7 / 2.0`, converts the other operand and gives 3.5.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a compile error?
options: int a = 3.7;
int b{3.7};
double c = 3;
unsigned char d{200};
questions.explanation: Braces reject narrowing: a double to an int inside braces is an error. The `=` form compiles and truncates, and the last line is a constant that fits.

questions.prompt: Why can `unsigned char c{300};` not compile?
options: char cannot be initialized with braces
300 does not fit in an unsigned char, which is a narrowing conversion
300 is an odd number
Braces only work with int
questions.explanation: A constant that does not fit the target type is a narrowing conversion, and list-initialization forbids it.

questions.prompt: What does the C-style cast `(T)x` do?
options: It always behaves like static_cast
It tries static_cast, then static_cast with const_cast, then reinterpret_cast, and uses the first that compiles
It behaves like dynamic_cast when it can
It checks the types at run time
questions.explanation: That fallback chain is the danger: a small mistake can silently turn into a const removal or a reinterpretation of raw bytes. A C-style cast never becomes a dynamic_cast.

questions.prompt: A `Base*` points to an object that is not a `Derived`. What does `static_cast<Derived*>(b)` do?
options: Returns nullptr
Throws bad_cast
Gives a pointer and the behavior is undefined when you use it
Does not compile
questions.explanation: A static downcast is unchecked: it just changes the pointer type. It is your promise that the object really is a Derived.

questions.prompt: What does `dynamic_cast<Derived&>(base)` do when `base` is not a Derived?
options: Returns a null reference
Throws std::bad_cast
Ignores the cast
Terminates the program immediately
questions.explanation: A reference cannot be null, so a failed reference cast throws `std::bad_cast`. The pointer form returns `nullptr` instead.

questions.prompt: What does `dynamic_cast` require of the base class?
options: A virtual function
A copy constructor
No data members
A template parameter
questions.explanation: Run-time type information lives with the vtable, so the base must be polymorphic: at least one virtual function.

questions.prompt: What is the problem with writing through a pointer produced by `const_cast` from a `const int` variable?
options: Nothing: const_cast makes the object writable
It is undefined behavior: the object itself is const
It copies the object first
It only works for pointers to classes
