questions.explanation: `const_cast` changes the type seen by the compiler, not the object. Modifying an object that was defined `const` is undefined behavior.

questions.prompt: Which is the safe way to reinterpret the bits of a `float` as a `uint32_t`?
options: reinterpret_cast on the pointer, then read it
std::memcpy or std::bit_cast
A C-style cast of the value
static_cast<std::uint32_t>(f)
questions.explanation: `static_cast` converts the number (1.0f becomes 1). Reading through a reinterpret_cast pointer breaks the aliasing rules. memcpy and bit_cast copy the bytes.

questions.prompt: A function takes `char*` but only reads, and you hold a `const char*`. Which cast fits?
options: reinterpret_cast
dynamic_cast
const_cast
static_cast
questions.explanation: Removing `const` for an API that does not write is the legitimate use of `const_cast`. Prefer fixing the API's signature if you own it.

questions.prompt: What is the default access of members in a `struct` versus a `class`?
options: Both private, because members default to private
Both public, because members default to public
struct is public by default, class is private
struct is private by default, class is public
questions.explanation: That is the only difference between them (it also applies to the default inheritance access).

questions.prompt: What does this print?
options: AB~B~A
BA~A~B
AB~A~B
B~BA~A
questions.explanation: Construction goes base first, then derived. Destruction is the exact reverse: derived first, then base.

questions.prompt: In what order are the members of a class initialized?
options: In the order of the initializer list: b_ then a_
In declaration order: a_ then b_
Alphabetical order
Unspecified
questions.explanation: Members are always initialized in the order they are declared in the class, whatever order the list is written in. Compilers warn with `-Wreorder`.

questions.prompt: Why is a member initializer list preferred over assigning in the constructor body?
options: It is required for every member of every class
It initializes members directly, and const and reference members need it
It makes the constructor explicit, so no implicit conversions happen
It runs before the base class constructor, so the base sees valid members
questions.explanation: Assigning in the body first default-constructs the member and then overwrites it. `const` and reference members cannot be assigned at all, so they must be in the list.

questions.prompt: What does a `const` member function promise?
options: That it returns a constant value that callers cannot modify
That it does not modify the object, so const objects can call it
That it is evaluated at compile time, like a constexpr function
That derived classes are not allowed to override it later on
questions.explanation: Inside a const member function `this` is a pointer to const, so members cannot be modified (unless marked `mutable`). Const objects can only call const member functions.

questions.prompt: What is a `static` data member?
options: A member stored separately inside every object
A single member shared by all objects of the class
A member that can never be changed
A member that is always stored on the stack
questions.explanation: There is exactly one copy for the whole class. It must be defined once outside the class (or declared `inline static` in C++17).

questions.prompt: What does `explicit` do on this constructor?
options: It only documents the intent and does not change behavior
walk(5.0) no longer compiles: no implicit conversion from double
It makes the constructor run faster by skipping a conversion step
It makes walk() a virtual function so derived classes can override it
questions.explanation: `explicit` forbids implicit conversions through that constructor. You must write `walk(Meters{5.0})`, which avoids accidental conversions.

questions.prompt: Which statement about `protected` members is correct?
options: Accessible by any code that can see the object, like a public member
Accessible inside the class and its derived classes, not from outside
Accessible only inside the class itself and not in derived classes
Accessible only from friends of the class
questions.explanation: `protected` sits between public and private: derived classes can use the member, outside code cannot.

questions.prompt: What is a class invariant?
options: A data member that is declared const and set once in the constructor
A rule every valid object satisfies, kept true by constructors and members
A member function that cannot be overridden in derived classes
A static data member that all objects of the class share
questions.explanation: For `BankAccount` it might be "the balance never goes negative". Hiding the representation and checking inputs in the public functions is how a class protects its invariant. If you cannot state one, the type is probably plain data and should be a `struct`.

questions.prompt: Where is the code of a member function stored when a program creates 1000 objects of the class?
options: Once, shared by all the objects
Once in each object, next to its data
Once in each object, but only if it is virtual
On the heap, one copy per object
questions.explanation: Objects carry only their data. A member function exists once; the hidden `this` pointer tells it which object to work on.

questions.prompt: What is `this` inside a member function?
options: A pointer to the object the function was called on
A copy of the object that the function was called on
A reference to the class itself, not to an object
A pointer to the first data member of the class
questions.explanation: `this` is the address of the current object. In a `const` member function it has type `const T*`.

questions.prompt: What is shared by all objects of a class?
options: A static data member, which exists once for the whole class
Every data member, because members belong to the class
Only the private data members of the class
Only the members that are declared const
questions.explanation: A `static` member belongs to the class, not to an object, so there is a single copy no matter how many objects exist.

questions.prompt: When does the destructor of a local object run?
options: At the closing brace of its scope, even if the scope is left by an exception
Only when you call delete on the object explicitly
When the program ends, after main has returned
When the object is last used, before the closing brace
questions.explanation: Local objects are destroyed when their scope ends, whatever way it ends. That guarantee is what RAII builds on.

questions.prompt: What goes wrong with this class when a copy is made?
options: The compiler-generated copy is correct for classes with pointers
It does not compile, because raw pointers cannot be copied by default
Both objects point at the same memory, so both destructors delete it
b becomes a reference to a, so changes to one show in the other
questions.explanation: The compiler-generated copy constructor is a shallow copy. This is why the Rule of Three exists: define a deep-copy constructor and assignment, or use `std::unique_ptr` / `std::vector` (Rule of Zero).

questions.prompt: The Rule of Three says that if a class needs a custom destructor, it probably also needs a custom...
options: Default constructor and move constructor
Copy constructor and copy assignment operator
Virtual function table and a virtual destructor
Static member and a friend declaration
questions.explanation: Destructor, copy constructor and copy assignment form the three. The Rule of Five adds the move constructor and move assignment. The Rule of Zero avoids all of them.

questions.prompt: Why must `operator<<` for printing a class be a non-member function?
options: Member operators cannot take references as parameters in C++
The left operand is std::ostream, which you cannot add members to
A member would be slower than a free function for stream output
Most operators in C++ must be declared as non-member functions
questions.explanation: A member operator has `*this` (your class) as its left operand. For `std::cout << obj` the left operand is the stream, so the function must be a free function (often a friend).

questions.prompt: What does `NoCopy(const NoCopy&) = delete;` do?
options: Deletes the object when it goes out of scope, instead of the destructor
Makes the class non-copyable: copying is a compile error
Calls the destructor on every copy attempt and then aborts the copy
Makes the class abstract so that it can no longer be created
questions.explanation: `= delete` removes the function. It is the modern way to forbid copying (for example for classes owning a unique resource).

questions.prompt: What happens on the last line?
options: It moves: the compiler generates a move constructor automatically
It copies: the declared destructor suppresses the move operations
It does not compile, because the move operations are deleted
Undefined behavior, because the source object is left empty
questions.explanation: A user-declared destructor (or copy operation) stops the compiler generating move operations, and an rvalue then falls back to the copy constructor. It compiles and works, just more slowly. Ask for the defaults with `= default` if the class should stay movable.

questions.prompt: What does declaring `explicit operator bool() const` allow?
options: Conversion operators cannot be declared explicit in C++
Use in conditions like if (obj), but not int n = obj; or obj + 1
Implicit conversion to bool everywhere, arithmetic included
Converting a bool value into an object of the class type
questions.explanation: An explicit conversion only applies where a bool is clearly wanted (if, while, !, &&, ||). Without explicit, a class convertible to bool also silently converts to int and takes part in arithmetic.

questions.prompt: What does `explicit` on a single-argument constructor prevent?
options: Copying the object from another object of the same class type
Implicit conversions from the argument type, such as Feet f = 3.0;
Inheritance from the class by other, completely unrelated types
Use of the class as an argument of any class template
questions.explanation: The conversion must be written out (`Feet(3.0)`). Mark single-argument constructors `explicit` by default.

questions.prompt: Why is `explicit operator bool()` better than a plain `operator bool()`?
options: It is faster, because the conversion is resolved at compile time
It works in if and while but not in arithmetic or other comparisons
It allows more conversions than a plain operator bool does
It avoids creating a vtable for the class, saving some memory
questions.explanation: A non-explicit `operator bool` converts to `int` and so lets `h + 1` or `h == 2` compile.

questions.prompt: What is the main benefit of copy-and-swap for `operator=`?
options: It is the fastest possible implementation of copy assignment in C++
The copy happens before *this changes: strong guarantee, safe self-assignment
It avoids calling the copy constructor entirely when assigning
It makes the class final so it cannot be derived from later
questions.explanation: The by-value parameter is the copy. If the copy throws, nothing has changed; then a non-throwing swap commits.

questions.prompt: What does the compiler-generated copy constructor do with a raw `int*` member?
options: Copies the pointer value, so both objects point to the same int
Allocates a new int and copies the value into it
Sets the pointer in the new object to nullptr
Does not compile until you write a copy constructor
questions.explanation: The default copy is member-wise and shallow: the address is copied, not the thing it points to. Two destructors then free the same block.

questions.prompt: Why can `operator<<` for printing a class not be a member function?
options: Its left operand is the stream, not an object of your class
Member functions cannot take a reference parameter
Operators that return a reference must be free functions
The standard forbids member operators on templates
questions.explanation: A member operator has `*this` as its left operand. For `os << v` the left operand is the `ostream`, so the function must be a non-member.

questions.prompt: A class holds a `std::vector<int>` and a `std::string` and nothing else. How many of the five special member functions should you write?
options: None: the Rule of Zero
Only the destructor
All five, to be safe
The copy pair, to make copies deep
questions.explanation: Both members already copy and move correctly and free their memory, so the compiler-generated versions are right. Write nothing.

options: Derived
Base
Compile error
Undefined behavior
questions.explanation: `f` is not virtual, so the call is bound at compile time from the pointer's static type (`Base*`). Making `Base::f` virtual would print "Derived". (The `Derived` is also leaked here.)

A virtual function that has two different overriders in a hierarchy
Two header files that include each other in a circle

questions.topic: Inheritance, Virtual Functions and the Object Model

questions.topic: Inheritance, Virtual Functions and the Object Model

questions.topic: Inheritance, Virtual Functions and the Object Model

The dynamic type of the object p points to
The pointer values stored in p and in a Dog*

questions.topic: Inheritance, Virtual Functions and the Object Model

Inside class templates that need access to the protected members of the base

questions.prompt: Why is `std::sort` with a lambda comparator usually faster than with a `std::function` comparator?

Lambdas are compiled to run on the graphics card instead
Both comparators run at exactly the same speed

To store callables of different types with one signature together
To make a call faster than the equivalent template would be
To capture variables by reference instead of by value

Only when it wraps a plain function pointer or a lambda
Each std::function allocates on the heap when constructed

questions.prompt: Why can a plain function pointer not carry a "limit" value for a comparison?

It is only an address: the function has no state besides arguments and globals
Functions cannot take int parameters, only pointers to them

questions.prompt: What is a functor?

A class with an operator(), so objects are callable and can hold state
Another name for a function pointer in older C++ code bases
A macro that expands to a lambda expression at compile time

questions.prompt: What does `int (*f)(int);` declare?

A pointer to an int that is named f here
An array of functions that take an int

questions.prompt: Which statement about a plain function pointer is true?
options: It can hold state in its own member variables
It is only an address, so it carries no state
It is always inlined by the compiler here
It can only point to member functions of classes
questions.explanation: A function pointer holds only the address of code. State must come from the arguments or from globals, which is why functors and lambdas exist.

questions.prompt: What makes `std::sort(v.begin(), v.end(), std::greater<>{})` cheap to run?

The comparator's type is known, so the call inlines
std::greater is implemented as a function pointer

questions.prompt: You need a vector that holds a mix of function pointers, functors and lambdas that all take an `int` and return an `int`. What type does the vector hold?

Calling the lambda from several threads safely at once

Lists cannot insert elements in the middle of the sequence

questions.prompt: What is the difference between `std::vector<int> a(3, 7);` and `std::vector<int> b{3, 7};`?

capacity counts only the elements that were erased

It does not compile: a pair cannot be unpacked
`lo` and `hi` are both pairs
questions.explanation: A structured binding names the members of the returned pair in order: `.first` becomes `lo` (1) and `.second` becomes `hi` (9).

questions.prompt: `auto [it, inserted] = m.insert({"a", 2});` where the map already holds the key "a" with value 1. What is `inserted`, and what does `it->second` read?
options: `true`, and 2
`false`, and 1
`false`, and 2
`true`, and 1
questions.explanation: `insert` never overwrites. It returns `pair<iterator, bool>`: the bool says whether a new element was added (`false` here), and the iterator points at the element that is in the map (still 1). Use `insert_or_assign` to overwrite.

questions.prompt: Which loop erases the even numbers correctly?
questions.code: std::vector<int> v{1, 2, 3, 4};
options: `for (auto it = v.begin(); it != v.end(); ++it) if (*it % 2 == 0) v.erase(it);`
`for (auto it = v.begin(); it != v.end(); ) { if (*it % 2 == 0) it = v.erase(it); else ++it; }`
`for (int x : v) if (x % 2 == 0) v.erase(&x);`
`v.erase(v.begin(), v.end(), 2);`
questions.explanation: `erase` invalidates the iterator and returns the next valid one. Using the return value (and not incrementing in that case) is the correct pattern. C++20 offers `std::erase_if(v, pred)`.

questions.prompt: Why does `std::sort(myList.begin(), myList.end())` fail to compile for a `std::list`?
options: Lists cannot hold int elements, just class types such as strings
std::sort needs random-access iterators; list has only bidirectional ones
std::sort works just on built-in arrays and std::array
The list would have to be declared const before sorting
questions.explanation: `sort` jumps around by index arithmetic. Use the member function `myList.sort()` instead.

questions.prompt: What does `end()` return for a container?
options: An iterator to the last element of the container
An iterator one past the last element, never dereferenced
A null pointer that marks the end of the container
An iterator to the first element of the container
questions.explanation: Ranges are half-open `[begin, end)`. `end()` is a sentinel position; dereferencing it is undefined behavior, and an empty container has `begin() == end()`.

questions.prompt: Why does `std::copy(src.begin(), src.end(), out.begin())` with an empty `out` break, and what fixes it?
options: It is fine: copy grows the destination automatically as it goes
It writes past the end; std::back_inserter(out) makes writes push_back
It needs std::move to work on empty destination containers
It needs just a reserve call on out before the copy starts
questions.explanation: Algorithms assign through the output iterator and do not grow the destination. An inserter turns assignments into insertions.

questions.prompt: Which function signature lets the caller pass a `std::vector<int>`, a C array `int[3]` or a slice of either, without a copy?
options: `long sum(const std::vector<int>& xs)`
`long sum(std::span<const int> xs)`
`long sum(int* xs)`
`long sum(std::vector<int> xs)`
questions.explanation: A span is a pointer plus a length over any contiguous elements. It accepts a vector, an array, a `std::array` or `subspan` of them, remembers its size, and is passed by value (two words).

questions.prompt: What is wrong here?
options: The span follows the vector automatically when it grows, so it stays valid
push_back may reallocate, leaving s pointing at freed memory
A span cannot be created from a std::vector, only from arrays
s[0] is bounds-checked and throws an exception on a bad index
questions.explanation: A view does not own its data. `push_back` can move the elements to a new buffer, leaving the span dangling. Take views for parameters and short-lived use, and re-create them after modifying the container.

questions.prompt: What does `v.end()` give for a non-empty vector?
options: An iterator one past the last element, never dereferenced
An iterator to the last element, which you may read and write
A null pointer that marks the end of the container
An iterator to a hidden sentinel element stored in the vector
questions.explanation: end() marks the position after the last element. The range is [begin, end), so end() itself is never dereferenced.

questions.prompt: Which iterator category lets you write `it + 3`?
options: Random access, as for vector and deque
Forward, as for forward_list and unordered containers
Bidirectional, as for list, map and set containers
Input, as for the iterators that read from streams
questions.explanation: Only random-access iterators support jumps and subtraction. A list has bidirectional iterators: ++ and --, no +n.

questions.prompt: Why is `for (auto it = c.begin(); it != c.end(); ++it)` preferred to `it < c.end()`?
options: `!=` works for every container; `<` does not
`<` is slower than `!=` on every container type
`<` is not allowed for pointers into an array
`!=` also checks the bounds of the container for you
questions.explanation: A list or map iterator has no operator<. The != test is the one every iterator category supports.

questions.prompt: What does `std::back_inserter(out)` give you?
options: An output iterator whose assignment calls push_back
A reverse iterator that walks the container backwards
An iterator that moves its elements instead of copying
A pointer to the last element currently stored in out
questions.explanation: Each assignment through it becomes a push_back, so the target grows as the algorithm writes.

questions.prompt: A `vector` has size 3 and capacity 3. What happens to `int* p = &v[0];` after `v.push_back(4)`?
options: It may dangle, because the vector reallocated
It stays valid because the element did not move
It points to the new first element
It becomes null
questions.explanation: A full vector allocates a bigger block, moves the elements and frees the old one. Pointers, references and iterators into it are invalid.

questions.prompt: What is the main risk of `std::string_view`?
options: It does not own the text, so it can dangle
It copies the whole text on every function call
It cannot be passed to functions as an argument
It always allocates its characters on the heap
questions.explanation: A view is a pointer and a length. The owner must outlive it.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explanation: Algorithms cannot change a container's size. `std::remove` only shifts elements and returns the new logical end. Combine it with `erase` (the erase-remove idiom) or use C++20 `std::erase`.

questions.prompt: Why must a sort comparator use `<` and not `<=`?
options: <= is slower than < for large ranges because it does extra work
The comparator must be a strict weak ordering: <= can crash std::sort
<= makes the sort unstable, so equal elements may be reordered
It is a style rule and has no effect on correctness
questions.explanation: Algorithms assume `comp(a, a)` is false. Violating that can cause out-of-bounds reads in `std::sort` and corrupt ordered containers.

questions.prompt: What must be true before calling `std::lower_bound` or `std::binary_search` on a range?
options: The range must contain no duplicate elements
The range must be sorted by the same ordering
The range must be stored in a std::vector
The range must not be empty before the call
questions.explanation: Binary search only makes sense on sorted data. On unsorted data the result is meaningless (and the precondition violation is undefined behavior).

questions.prompt: What does `v | std::views::filter(f) | std::views::transform(g)` do when it is created?
options: It builds a new vector right away from the filtered values
Nothing yet: it is a lazy view, evaluated when iterated
It sorts v in place before elements are read
It copies every element of v into a temporary vector
questions.explanation: Views are lazy and non-owning. Work happens during iteration, with no temporary containers.

questions.prompt: What is the practical difference between `std::sort(v.begin(), v.end())` and `std::ranges::sort(v)`?
options: The ranges version is faster than the iterator version of sort
The ranges version takes the whole container (and supports projections)
The ranges version works on built-in arrays, not on vectors
You can write the same things with both, in code
questions.explanation: The ranges algorithms accept a whole range, so you cannot mismatch begin and end of different containers, and they support projections such as `std::ranges::sort(people, {}, &Person::age)`. The sorting itself is the same.

questions.prompt: When can a view such as `v | std::views::filter(f)` become a dangling problem?
options: Not a problem: a view owns a private copy of the data it shows
When the container dies or reallocates while the view is still used
When the filter function returns false for all elements
With transform, not with filter, since filter is lazy
questions.explanation: A view is non-owning, like `string_view`. If the vector dies, or reallocates after a `push_back`, the view points at stale memory.

questions.prompt: Two engines are created as `std::mt19937 a(42), b(42);` and used with the same distribution. What do they produce?
options: Different sequences, because each engine is random
The same sequence: same seed, same numbers
An error: the seed must come from std::random_device
Zeros, since the seeds are equal
questions.explanation: An engine is deterministic: the same seed gives the same sequence (compiled: true). That is what you want in tests and simulations; use `std::random_device` to seed when you want different runs.

questions.prompt: Why is `rand() % 6 + 1` a poor way to roll a die in modern C++?
options: It is too slow to matter in everyday modern code
A weak generator, modulo bias and hidden global state
It does not compile when used with modern C++ headers
It produces the value 0 on most platforms
questions.explanation: Use an engine plus a distribution (`std::mt19937` with `std::uniform_int_distribution<int>(1, 6)`): better quality, no modulo bias, and no global state.

questions.prompt: What does `std::remove(v.begin(), v.end(), 3)` do to `v.size()`?
options: Nothing: it only shifts kept elements forward
It shrinks the vector by the number of 3s it found
It throws an exception if there is no 3 in the range
It sets the removed slots to zero and keeps the size
questions.explanation: Algorithms work through iterators and cannot change the size of a container. Erase the tail afterwards: erase-remove.

questions.prompt: What is wrong with `std::accumulate(v.begin(), v.end(), 0)` when `v` holds doubles?
options: The int start value makes the sum an int
It does not compile when the range holds doubles
It sums only the first half of the range given to it
It needs a custom lambda to be able to add doubles
questions.explanation: The type of the initial value decides the type of the sum. Write 0.0.

questions.prompt: How do you find a key in a `std::map` efficiently?
options: Call the member `m.find(key)`, O(log n)
Call `std::find(m.begin(), m.end(), key)` on the map
Loop over the whole map and compare every key by hand
Sort the map first and then call lower_bound on it
questions.explanation: std::find walks every element in O(n) and compares pairs. The member function uses the tree.

questions.prompt: Why does `std::transform` into an empty vector need `std::back_inserter`?
options: It writes through the output iterator without growing
transform sorts the output container before writing
back_inserter makes the lambda run noticeably faster
An empty vector does not have a begin() iterator
questions.explanation: Algorithms assign through iterators. An inserter turns each assignment into a push_back.

questions.prompt: What does the projection in `std::ranges::sort(people, {}, &Person::age)` do?
options: It sorts by the age member, no comparator needed
It copies all the ages into a new temporary vector
It sorts the data members inside every Person object
It sorts the people in descending order of their age
questions.explanation: A projection is applied to each element before the comparison. The empty braces select the default less.

questions.prompt: What does `std::unique` do to the vector {1, 2, 1, 2}?
options: It removes nothing, because there are no neighbouring duplicates
It removes the second 1 and the second 2
It sorts the vector and then removes the duplicates
It removes the first element of each pair of duplicates
questions.explanation: unique removes only equal neighbours. Sort first when you want every duplicate gone.

questions.prompt: Which algorithm puts the elements that satisfy a predicate in front and returns the split point?
options: `std::partition`
`std::sort`
`std::find_if`
`std::accumulate`
questions.explanation: partition reorders the range so matches come first and returns an iterator to the first non-match.

questions.prompt: Why is `std::find(m.begin(), m.end(), key)` a poor way to look up a key in a `map`?
options: It scans every element in O(n) and the member find uses the tree in O(log n)
It does not compile for maps at all
It returns the value instead of an iterator
It modifies the map when the key is missing
questions.explanation: The generic algorithm knows nothing about the tree. The member find is the fast path.

questions.prompt: What does the compiler do with a function template when you call it with a new type?
options: Templates are resolved at run time by a hidden lookup
It instantiates a concrete function for those arguments and compiles it
It builds a virtual function table for the call to dispatch through
It converts the arguments to a common base type before calling
questions.explanation: A template is only a blueprint. Each distinct set of template arguments causes a new function (or class) to be generated at compile time.

questions.prompt: Why does this fail to compile?
options: maxOf needs a third parameter to decide which type should be compared
Deduction conflict: T is int from one argument and double from the other
A double cannot be compared with an int by the language rules
Templates cannot be called with literal values like 3 and 2.5
questions.explanation: Both parameters share one `T`, but the arguments deduce `int` and `double`. Fix with `maxOf<double>(3, 2.5)` or by using two template parameters.

questions.prompt: What is the problem with `maxOf("apple", "pear")` for the same template?
options: It does not compile: arrays cannot be arguments
It compiles but compares the pointers, not the text
It returns an empty string without comparing
It throws an exception for string literals
questions.explanation: The string literals decay to `const char*`, so `a < b` compares addresses. Use `std::string` or `std::string_view`.

questions.prompt: In `template <typename T> void f(T&& x);` what is `T&&`?
options: An rvalue reference to T, binding to temporaries and not to lvalues
A forwarding reference: it binds lvalues and rvalues and remembers which
A compile error: references to references are illegal in C++
A pointer to a pointer to T, spelled with reference syntax here
questions.explanation: When `T` is deduced for that function, `T&&` is a forwarding (universal) reference. It is a real rvalue reference only for something like `void g(Widget&&)` or `std::vector<T>&&`.

questions.prompt: If `int x = 1;` and you call `f(x)` for `template <typename T> void f(T&& p);`, what is `T`?
options: int
int&
int&&
const int
questions.explanation: For an lvalue argument, `T` is deduced as `int&`. Reference collapsing then turns `int& &&` into `int&`, so `p` is an lvalue reference.

questions.prompt: What does reference collapsing do with `T&& &&`?
options: Collapses to T&
Collapses to T&&
Is an error
Collapses to T
questions.explanation: If either side is an lvalue reference the result is an lvalue reference. Only rvalue-reference-to-rvalue-reference stays an rvalue reference.

questions.prompt: What does this compute?
options: A tuple holding the values (1, 2, 3, 4)
10, via a C++17 fold expression
A compile error because the pack is empty
4, the number of elements in the pack
questions.explanation: `(args + ...)` is a unary right fold: `1 + (2 + (3 + 4))`. The size of the pack is `sizeof...(args)`.

questions.prompt: What does `sizeof...(Args)` return?
options: The total size in bytes of all arguments
The number of elements in the parameter pack
The size in bytes of the first argument
It is not valid C++ outside of variadic function templates
questions.explanation: It counts the elements of the pack, at compile time. It is not the same as `sizeof`.

questions.prompt: Why does a dependent type name like `T::iterator` need the `typename` keyword inside a template?
options: It is a style convention and can be omitted
Until T is known, the compiler cannot tell a type from a value
typename speeds up name lookup inside templates
It lets the nested type take part in multiple inheritance
questions.explanation: Without `typename`, `T::iterator` is assumed to be a value. Write `typename T::iterator it = c.begin();`.

questions.prompt: What is a common drawback of heavy template use?
options: Run-time slowdown caused by virtual calls in the instantiations
Longer compile times, bigger binaries and hard-to-read errors
Memory leaks in the instantiations of a class template
Templates cannot be inlined by modern optimizing compilers
questions.explanation: Each instantiation is separate code, and errors surface inside instantiations. The upside is zero runtime overhead and aggressive inlining.

questions.prompt: Which is the best description of templates compared with virtual functions?
options: Templates are run-time polymorphism, exactly like virtual functions are
Templates resolve at compile time with no indirection; virtual calls at run time
They are the same mechanism with different syntax and different names
Virtual functions are faster, because compilers inline them
questions.explanation: With templates the concrete type is resolved when compiling (so calls can be inlined), but the set of types is fixed then. Virtual dispatch decides at runtime at the cost of an indirection.

questions.prompt: Which of these declarations is a forwarding (universal) reference?
options: `template <class T> void f(T&& x);`
`template <class T> void f(const T&& x);`
`template <class T> void f(std::vector<T>&& v);`
`void f(Widget&& w);`
questions.explanation: It must be exactly `T&&` (or `auto&&`) with the type deduced for that function. A `const` qualifier, a wrapper such as `vector<T>`, a fixed type like `Widget`, or a `T` fixed by the enclosing class all make it an ordinary rvalue reference.

questions.prompt: For `template <typename T> void f(T x);` called as `f(ci)` with `const int ci`, what is `T`?
options: `const int`
`int`
`const int&`
`int&`
questions.explanation: A by-value parameter is a copy, so top-level `const` and references are dropped from the deduced type.

questions.prompt: For `template <typename T> void f(T& x);` called as `f(ci)` with `const int ci`, what is `T`?
options: `int`
`const int`
`int&`
It fails to compile
questions.explanation: A reference parameter must keep the argument's `const`, so `T` is `const int` and the parameter is `const int&`.

questions.prompt: Why does `maxOf(3, 2.5)` fail for `template <typename T> T maxOf(T a, T b)`?
options: T is deduced as both int and double, and deduction does not convert
Templates cannot be instantiated with double arguments
The return type cannot be deduced from the two arguments
It compiles and silently returns 3 as an int, truncating
questions.explanation: Each argument deduces its own `T` and they conflict. Specify `maxOf<double>(3, 2.5)` or use two template parameters.

questions.prompt: What does `std::vector v{1, 2, 3};` deduce (C++17)?
options: It does not compile without the template argument spelled out
`std::vector<int>`, by class template argument deduction
std::vector<std::initializer_list<int>>, holding one element
std::vector<long>, because the literals are widened
questions.explanation: CTAD deduces the class's template arguments from the constructor call.

questions.prompt: An `int arr[3]` is passed to `template <typename T> void f(T x);`. What is `T`?
options: `int*`
`int&`
questions.explanation: By-value deduction makes arrays decay to pointers. Take `T (&x)[N]` or `T&` to keep the array type.

questions.prompt: Where should the full definition of a function template normally go?
options: In a .cpp file, to keep the header small and compile faster
In the header, so each translation unit that instantiates it sees the body
In a separate .o file that is linked in at a later stage
Anywhere, since the compiler and linker treat all placements alike
questions.explanation: The compiler needs the body at the point of instantiation. A body hidden in a .cpp file leads to linker errors (unless you use explicit instantiation there).

questions.prompt: What is a non-type template parameter?
questions.code:
template <typename T, std::size_t N>
struct Buffer { T data[N]; };
options: A parameter that is not allowed to be a class template
A compile-time constant value such as N used as a template argument
A parameter that cannot be deduced by the compiler from the call
A parameter passed by reference to the template instead of by value
questions.explanation: `N` is a value known at compile time, which is how `std::array<int, 5>` encodes its size in its type.

questions.prompt: Which statement about partial specialization is true?
options: It is allowed for function templates as well as for class templates
It is allowed for class templates, not function templates (overload instead)
It is not allowed for templates in standard C++ code
It is allowed only when every template parameter is a non-type parameter
questions.explanation: Class templates can be partially specialized (for example `Foo<T*>`). Function templates cannot, so you overload them.

questions.prompt: What can an alias template do that a `typedef` cannot?
options: They are two spellings of the same feature
Take template parameters of its own
Create a brand new distinct type
Be used in header files without a definition
questions.explanation: `template <typename T> using Vec = std::vector<T>;` is a family of aliases. A `typedef` names one concrete type.

questions.prompt: What is `std::make_index_sequence<3>` used for?
options: Creating an array of three integers filled at run time
Generating the pack 0, 1, 2 at compile time to expand per index
Shuffling three indices into a random order at run time
Counting how many worker threads are currently running
questions.explanation: It produces `std::index_sequence<0, 1, 2>`; a function template deduces the pack `I...` and expands `get<I>(t)...`.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a variable template?
options: `template <typename T> constexpr T zero = T{};`
`template <typename T> using Zero = T;` an alias template
`template <typename T> T zero();` a function template
`constexpr int zero = 0;` an ordinary variable
questions.explanation: A variable template gives one variable per `T` (`zero<int>`, `zero<double>`). The standard's `std::is_integral_v<T>` is defined this way.

questions.prompt: In `template <template <typename...> class C, typename T> C<T> make(T a, T b);`, what do you pass for `C`?
options: A concrete type such as std::vector<int>, with its argument
A template such as std::vector, without arguments
A function pointer to a factory function that builds C
An integer that selects which container kind to build
questions.explanation: A template template parameter takes a template: `make<std::vector>(3, 4)` builds a `std::vector<int>`.

questions.prompt: What is `N` in `template <typename T, std::size_t N> class Buffer`?
options: A non-type parameter: a compile-time value
A second type parameter given to the template
A runtime argument passed to the constructor
A default member initializer for the class template
questions.explanation: Buffer<int, 4> and Buffer<int, 8> are different types, which is how std::array knows its size.

questions.prompt: Where should the member function definitions of a class template normally live?
options: In the header, visible to every instantiation
In a .cpp file, to keep the header file small
In a separate library that is linked in later
Nowhere: they are generated by the compiler itself
questions.explanation: The compiler needs the body to instantiate the class for each set of arguments. A body in a .cpp gives linker errors.

questions.prompt: What does `std::vector v{1, 2, 3};` deduce?
options: `std::vector<int>`, by argument deduction
`std::vector<double>`, the widest of the types
Nothing: it does not compile before C++20 at all
`std::vector<auto>`, which is resolved at run time
questions.explanation: Since C++17 the compiler deduces the class template arguments from the constructor call.

questions.prompt: Which specialization is chosen for `Info<char*>` if there are a primary template, a partial `Info<T*>` and a full `Info<char*>`?
options: The full specialization `Info<char*>`
The partial specialization `Info<T*>`
The primary template
It is ambiguous and does not compile
questions.explanation: The most specialized match wins: full, then partial, then the primary template.

questions.prompt: What is an alias template?
options: A parameterized using for a family of types
A second name that refers to a function template
A class template that has a default argument
A template that is defined inside another template
questions.explanation: An alias template names a family of types. You cannot do that with a plain typedef.

questions.topic: Type Traits, Concepts and Compile-time C++
questions.prompt: What is a type trait?
options: A run-time property that is stored in each object of the type
A template in <type_traits> that queries or transforms a type at compile time
A keyword that marks a class as final, so it cannot be a base class
A debugging flag that records the names of all types at run time
questions.explanation: Traits like `std::is_integral<T>` and `std::remove_reference<T>` are evaluated entirely by the compiler.

questions.topic: Type Traits, Concepts and Compile-time C++
questions.prompt: What is the C++17 shorthand for `std::is_integral<T>::value`?
options: `std::is_integral<T>()`
`std::is_integral_t<T>`
`std::is_integral_v<T>`
`std::integral<T>`
questions.explanation: `_v` is the variable template for `::value`. `_t` is the alias for `::type` on transformation traits like `remove_reference_t`.

questions.topic: Type Traits, Concepts and Compile-time C++
questions.prompt: What does `std::is_same_v<int, const int>` evaluate to?
options: true
false
A compile error
It depends on the compiler
questions.explanation: Top-level `const` is part of the type, so `int` and `const int` are different types.

questions.topic: Type Traits, Concepts and Compile-time C++
questions.prompt: What does `std::is_integral_v<const int>` evaluate to?
options: true
false
A compile error
Only true in C++20
questions.explanation: `is_integral` ignores cv-qualifiers, so `const int` is still an integral type.

questions.topic: Type Traits, Concepts and Compile-time C++
questions.prompt: What does `std::is_integral_v<int&>` evaluate to?
options: true
false
A compile error
true, because a reference to int behaves like int
questions.explanation: A reference type is a different kind of type from the integral type it refers to. Use `std::remove_reference_t` (or `remove_cvref_t`) first.

questions.topic: Type Traits, Concepts and Compile-time C++
questions.prompt: What is the difference between `static_assert` and `assert`?
options: They are the same check, apart from the spelling
static_assert is checked at compile time; assert runs at run time unless NDEBUG
assert is checked at compile time, while static_assert runs at run time
static_assert works inside header files, assert in sources
questions.explanation: `static_assert` needs a constant expression and fails the build; `assert` checks while the program runs.

questions.topic: Type Traits, Concepts and Compile-time C++
questions.prompt: What does SFINAE stand for?
options: Safe Function Inlining And Naming Extension
Substitution Failure Is Not An Error
Static Function Instantiation And Name Elaboration
Selective Failure In Namespace Evaluation
questions.explanation: If substituting template arguments into a candidate produces an invalid type, that candidate is quietly dropped from overload resolution.

questions.topic: Type Traits, Concepts and Compile-time C++
questions.prompt: In this code, which overload does `print(2.5)` call?
options: Ambiguous: compile error
Neither
questions.explanation: For `double` the condition of (1) is false, so `enable_if_t` has no `::type` and that overload is discarded by SFINAE. Only (2) remains.

questions.topic: Type Traits, Concepts and Compile-time C++
questions.prompt: Why is `if constexpr` often better than `enable_if` for choosing code by type?
options: It runs faster than enable_if at run time, since it skips overloads
One readable function body, and the discarded branch is not instantiated
It works in C++98 compilers as well as in newer ones
It allows run-time conditions inside templates, unlike enable_if
questions.explanation: You write one function with a compile-time branch instead of several overloads, and code in the false branch need not compile for that type.

questions.topic: Type Traits, Concepts and Compile-time C++
questions.prompt: What goes wrong with an ordinary `if (std::is_integral_v<T>)` inside a template?
options: It is a syntax error inside a template body
Both branches must compile for every T, even the one that never runs
It is evaluated at run time, so it is slower than if constexpr
It behaves exactly like if constexpr in a template
questions.explanation: A plain `if` is run-time, so both branches are always compiled. Code that is invalid for some `T` breaks the build unless you use `if constexpr`.

questions.topic: Type Traits, Concepts and Compile-time C++
questions.prompt: Which statement about a `constexpr` function is correct?
options: It is evaluated at compile time, whatever its arguments
It may run at compile time for constant arguments, and also at run time
It can only be called from main and from other constexpr functions
It cannot take parameters, since it must be a constant
questions.explanation: `constexpr` allows compile-time evaluation; it does not force it. Use a `constexpr` variable or `consteval` to guarantee it.

questions.topic: Type Traits, Concepts and Compile-time C++
questions.prompt: What does `consteval` (C++20) add?
options: A faster version of constexpr that skips some checks
Every call must be evaluated at compile time, or it is an error
The function runs at run time and not in constants
It makes a variable mutable inside constant expressions
questions.explanation: A `consteval` function is an immediate function. A call with a non-constant argument is ill-formed.

questions.topic: Type Traits, Concepts and Compile-time C++
questions.prompt: What does `constinit` guarantee?
options: The variable is const and can never be modified
The variable is initialised at compile time but can change later
The variable lives in read-only memory and cannot be changed
The variable is thread-local, with one copy for each thread
questions.explanation: `constinit` fixes the static-initialisation-order problem by requiring constant initialisation, without making the variable immutable.

questions.topic: Type Traits, Concepts and Compile-time C++
questions.prompt: In the classic template-metaprogramming factorial, what stops the recursion?
questions.code:
template <int N> struct Fact { static constexpr int value = Fact<N-1>::value * N; };
// ???
options: A static_assert inside the struct that stops at a limit
A full specialisation template <> struct Fact<0> with value = 1
A virtual function that returns early when N reaches 0
The compiler stops at 256 levels and gives a valid result
questions.explanation: The specialisation for 0 provides the base case. Without it the compiler keeps instantiating `Fact<-1>`, `Fact<-2>`... until it hits its recursion limit.

questions.topic: Type Traits, Concepts and Compile-time C++
questions.prompt: Which is the modern replacement for computing a value with recursive template structs?
options: A preprocessor macro with arguments
A constexpr function
A virtual function in a base class
A global lookup table built at start-up
questions.explanation: Ordinary-looking `constexpr` functions are shorter, more readable and can also be used at run time.

questions.topic: Type Traits, Concepts and Compile-time C++
questions.prompt: What is a C++20 concept?
options: A run-time check that throws an exception when it fails
A named compile-time condition on template arguments
A kind of virtual base class used for interfaces
A macro that expands to an enable_if expression
questions.explanation: A concept is a compile-time boolean over types, such as `std::integral<T>`, that constrains a template. A call with a type that does not satisfy it is rejected at the call site with a readable message.

questions.topic: Type Traits, Concepts and Compile-time C++
questions.prompt: What happens here?
options: It returns 5.0, since the double is simply doubled
It returns 4, the double truncated to an integer
A compile error: std::integral<double> is not satisfied
A run-time exception thrown from inside the function
questions.explanation: A `double` is not integral, so the constrained template is not a candidate and the call fails to compile with a message that names the unmet constraint. Without the concept the function would happily return 5.0.

questions.topic: Type Traits, Concepts and Compile-time C++
questions.prompt: In `requires(T a, T b) { { a + b } -> std::convertible_to<T>; }`, what does the part in braces express?
options: That a + b must compile and give a result convertible to T
That a and b must be equal for the expression to compile
That + must be commutative for all pairs of values
That T must be an integer type, not a class type
questions.explanation: A requires-expression lists operations that must be valid; `{ expr } -> Concept` also constrains the type of the result. It checks syntax and types only, not mathematical properties such as commutativity.

questions.topic: Type Traits, Concepts and Compile-time C++
questions.prompt: What is special about `if constexpr`?
options: It evaluates its condition at run time, only a little faster than if
The condition is evaluated at compile time and the other branch is discarded
It can only be used outside of templates, in ordinary functions
It compiles and executes both branches in the order written
questions.explanation: That is what lets one template body use operations that are valid for some types only, with a different branch chosen for each instantiation.

questions.topic: Type Traits, Concepts and Compile-time C++
questions.prompt: What is the main advantage of C++20 concepts over `enable_if`?
options: They make the generated code run faster than enable_if code
They state requirements directly and give clear, early error messages
They remove the need for templates altogether in generic code
They are evaluated at run time, not at compile time
questions.explanation: `template <std::integral T>` documents the constraint in the signature and produces "constraint not satisfied" instead of a wall of instantiation errors.

questions.prompt: What does RAII stand for, and what is its core idea?
options: Resource Allocation Is Immediate: allocate everything at start-up
Resource Acquisition Is Initialization: an object's lifetime owns the resource
Run At Initialization Instantly: run code before main starts
Reference And Instance Isolation: keep objects apart from references
questions.explanation: Acquire in the constructor, release in the destructor. Because destructors run on scope exit, even during exceptions, resources cannot leak.

questions.prompt: What is the output?
options: open caught
open close caught
open caught close
close caught open
questions.explanation: Stack unwinding destroys `g` (printing "close") while the exception propagates out of `f`, before the catch block runs.

questions.prompt: What happens if a destructor throws while the stack is already unwinding from another exception?
options: The second exception is ignored and unwinding continues
std::terminate is called and the program ends
Both exceptions are caught together by the same handler
The second exception replaces the first, which is lost
questions.explanation: Two active exceptions cannot be handled, so C++ calls `std::terminate`. That is why destructors must not let exceptions escape.

questions.prompt: How should you catch exceptions?
options: By value, so the handler owns its own copy of the exception
By const reference, avoiding copies and slicing
By pointer, so nothing is copied and the object can be shared
By rvalue reference, so the handler can move from it
questions.explanation: Catching by value copies and slices derived exception types. `catch (const std::exception& e)` is the standard idiom.

questions.prompt: Which of these is NOT an RAII type?
options: std::lock_guard, which unlocks its mutex in the destructor
std::fstream, which closes its file in the destructor
A raw FILE* returned by fopen, closed by hand
std::unique_ptr, which deletes its object in the destructor
questions.explanation: A raw `FILE*` must be closed by hand with `fclose`, so an early return or exception leaks it. The other three release their resource in a destructor.

questions.prompt: A scope guard holds a rollback action. What does calling `release()` on it before the end of the scope do?
options: Runs the rollback immediately
Cancels the rollback: the work is committed
Throws an exception to signal the commit
Runs the rollback twice, once now and once later
questions.explanation: The guard's destructor only runs the cleanup while it is still active. `release()` deactivates it once the work has succeeded.

questions.prompt: What does the Rule of Zero say?
options: Give every class a default constructor and no other constructor
Use RAII members, so no destructor, copy or move needs writing by hand
Delete the copy constructor of each class you write
Classes must have zero data members to stay in a valid state
questions.explanation: If every member manages itself (`vector`, `string`, `unique_ptr`), the compiler-generated special members are correct and you write none.

questions.prompt: Inside a `catch` block, what is the difference between `throw;` and `throw e;`?
options: They are identical, since both rethrow the exception
throw; rethrows the original; throw e; throws a copy and can slice
throw; terminates the program immediately by calling std::terminate
throw e; rethrows the same object without making any copy
questions.explanation: Use a bare `throw;` to rethrow. Throwing the caught variable copies it and loses the derived part when the handler's type is a base.

questions.prompt: A constructor throws halfway through. Which destructors run?
options: None: the object never existed, so nothing is destroyed
Members and bases already built, but not the object's own destructor
The object's own destructor, plus those of all of its members
Those of every member, including members not yet constructed
questions.explanation: The object never finished construction, so its own destructor does not run. Already-built subobjects are destroyed, which is why members should be RAII types.

questions.prompt: What is printed?
options: A
B
AB
The code does not compile
questions.explanation: Handlers are tried in order and the first match wins. `invalid_argument` derives from `exception`, so the first handler catches it and the second can never run. Put the more specific handler first.

questions.prompt: Which guarantee does "if the operation throws, the object is exactly as before" describe?
options: No-throw guarantee
Strong guarantee
Basic guarantee
No guarantee
questions.explanation: Commit or rollback is the strong guarantee. The basic guarantee only promises no leaks and valid invariants; the no-throw guarantee means it never throws.

questions.prompt: Why does this give the strong guarantee?
options: The copy happens first and swap cannot throw, so rows_ is untouched on failure
swap rolls the vector back automatically if it throws halfway through
The parameter is const, so no error can happen inside the function
std::vector is thread-safe, so no partial update can be observed
questions.explanation: All the work that can fail (the copy) happens on a temporary. The commit is a non-throwing swap, so any exception leaves `*this` unchanged.

questions.prompt: What happens when a function marked `noexcept` throws?
options: `std::terminate` is called
The caller catches it as usual
The exception is silently ignored
It is undefined behaviour with no defined outcome
questions.explanation: A `noexcept` function does not propagate exceptions: leaving it with one calls `std::terminate`. Only promise `noexcept` when it is true.

questions.prompt: A class has a move constructor not marked `noexcept` (and a copy constructor). What does `std::vector` do when it grows?
options: Moves the elements anyway, accepting the risk
Copies the elements, to keep the strong guarantee
Calls std::terminate as soon as it has to grow
Fails to compile, since the move may throw
questions.explanation: `vector` uses `std::move_if_noexcept`: it only moves if the move cannot throw, otherwise it copies. Mark moves `noexcept` to avoid silent copies on every reallocation.

questions.prompt: Which of these is `noexcept` by default?
options: A destructor
A user-written move constructor
A user-written copy constructor
Every function that does not contain `throw`
questions.explanation: Destructors are implicitly `noexcept`. Other functions, including your own move constructor, may throw unless you say otherwise.

questions.prompt: What is the main problem with this class?
options: It can be copied, so two objects would fclose the same handle
fclose cannot be called from a destructor
The constructor has to be private
fopen allocates its result on the stack
questions.explanation: The compiler-generated copy copies the pointer, so both objects close the same `FILE*`. Delete the copy operations (and add moves if needed), or hold the handle in a `std::unique_ptr` with a custom deleter.

questions.prompt: What is the output?
options: +A+B-B-A
+A+B-A-B
+B+A-A-B
+A-A+B-B
questions.explanation: Locals are destroyed in the reverse order of construction, so `b` goes before `a`. This is why a guard declared later can safely rely on one declared earlier.

questions.prompt: What is the output?
options: +X-Xcaught
+Xcaught-X
+Xcaught
caught+X-X
questions.explanation: While the exception travels up the stack, `g` is destroyed (stack unwinding). That happens before the handler's body runs, so `-X` comes before `caught`.

questions.prompt: How should an RAII class that owns one unique resource handle copying?
options: Delete the copy operations and provide move operations
Keep the compiler's copy so both objects share the handle
Copy the handle and let only the first destructor release it
Make the destructor virtual
questions.explanation: One owner means one release. Deleting the copy and providing a move transfers ownership, which is how `std::unique_ptr` and `std::thread` behave.

questions.prompt: What is wrong with this function?
options: If work() throws, delete[] never runs and the memory leaks
It must use delete instead of delete[]
new int[100] is not allowed inside a function
p has to be declared const
questions.explanation: A manual `new` and `delete` pair breaks on any early exit. Use `std::vector<int>` or `std::unique_ptr<int[]>` so the destructor does the release.

questions.prompt: What is the output?
options: work close2 close1
work close1 close2
close1 close2 work
work
questions.explanation: The deleter runs when each `unique_ptr` is destroyed, after `work` is printed. Locals are destroyed in reverse order, so `b` closes first.

questions.prompt: A destructor of a local object still runs when the scope is left by an exception.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: That is stack unwinding, and it is the reason RAII works. The one exception is a program that ends in `std::terminate`, where unwinding may not happen.

questions.prompt: `std::lock_guard` is an RAII type: it unlocks the mutex in its destructor.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: It locks in the constructor and unlocks in the destructor, so the mutex is released even if the code in between throws.

questions.prompt: What is the output?
options: base
derived
base derived
It does not compile
questions.explanation: Handlers are tried in the order written and the first compatible one runs. `runtime_error` derives from `exception`, so the second handler is unreachable (compilers usually warn). Put the most derived handler first.

questions.prompt: What goes wrong if `new` throws inside this assignment operator?
options: data_ still points at the deleted array, so the object is broken
The old data is restored automatically
The program is guaranteed to terminate
n_ is reset to zero automatically
questions.explanation: The old array was released before the new one existed. Allocate and copy first, then release the old data, or use copy-and-swap, to get the strong guarantee.

questions.prompt: What does the copy-and-swap idiom give you?
options: The strong guarantee, because the only step that can throw happens on the copy before anything changes
The nothrow guarantee for every operation
Faster assignment than copying in place
Automatic move semantics
questions.explanation: If copying the argument throws, `*this` has not been touched yet. The final swap does not throw, so the assignment either fully succeeds or changes nothing.

questions.prompt: What is the output?
options: inner outer
inner
outer
outer inner
questions.explanation: `throw;` with no operand rethrows the exception currently being handled, so the outer handler gets the original `int`.

questions.prompt: What happens if an exception is thrown and no handler catches it?
options: std::terminate is called and the program aborts
main returns 1 and the program ends normally
The exception is silently ignored
The next function call in main handles it
questions.explanation: With no matching handler, `std::terminate` runs. It is implementation-defined whether the stack is unwound first, so destructors may not run.

questions.prompt: What can go wrong here?
options: If work() throws, the mutex stays locked and later callers block forever
unlock must be called before lock
A mutex cannot be a global variable
work() cannot be called while locked
questions.explanation: Use `std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lock(m);` so the unlock happens in a destructor on every path, including an exception.

questions.prompt: Which operation must not throw for copy-and-swap to give the strong guarantee?
options: swap
The copy constructor
operator new
The destructor of the copy's source
questions.explanation: The swap is the commit step. Anything that can throw has to happen before it, on the copy. That is why swap functions are marked `noexcept`.

questions.prompt: A destructor should never let an exception escape.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Destructors are `noexcept` by default. If one throws while the stack is already unwinding, the program calls `std::terminate`.

questions.prompt: What is the output?
questions.explanation: The `noexcept(expr)` operator reports at compile time whether the expression is declared non-throwing. `f` is, `g` is not.

questions.prompt: What happens when this program runs?
options: std::terminate is called and nothing is printed
caught
It does not compile
caught, then the program terminates
questions.explanation: An exception that leaves a `noexcept` function calls `std::terminate`. The handler in `main` never gets a chance. Compilers usually warn about the throw.

questions.prompt: When is `std::move_if_noexcept` useful?
options: It moves only when the move constructor cannot throw, otherwise it copies, so the strong guarantee holds
It forces a move even if the move may throw
It makes a function noexcept
It catches exceptions thrown during a move
questions.explanation: If a move could throw halfway, the source would already be damaged. `vector` growth uses this rule: it moves elements only when the move is `noexcept`, else it copies.

questions.prompt: Which is the best use of an exception?
options: Reporting that a file the program needs cannot be opened
Leaving a loop as soon as a value is found
Returning a second result from a function
Detecting the end of a file while reading lines
questions.explanation: Exceptions fit rare failures that the caller cannot handle locally. Ordinary outcomes, like "not found" or "end of input", belong in return values, `std::optional` or `std::expected`.

questions.prompt: This swap only exchanges a pointer and an integer. What should be added?
options: noexcept, so copy-and-swap and containers can rely on it
virtual
const after the parameter list
static
questions.explanation: A swap of pointers and integers cannot fail, so say so with `noexcept`. Generic code checks that promise to choose the faster, safer path.

questions.prompt: What is the output?
options: bad state
std::exception
logic_error
Nothing is printed
questions.explanation: Catching by const reference keeps the real type, so the virtual `what()` returns the message passed to the constructor.

questions.prompt: Destructors are implicitly noexcept in C++11 and later.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Unless a member or base class has a potentially-throwing destructor, or you write `noexcept(false)`, a destructor is `noexcept` by default.

questions.prompt: A noexcept function is not allowed to call a function that may throw.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: It may, and the compiler accepts it. If the exception then escapes the `noexcept` function, `std::terminate` is called, so the function must handle it inside.

questions.topic: Values or Errors: optional, variant and expected
questions.prompt: Which failure is best reported with a return value (`std::optional` or an error code) rather than an exception?
options: A parser rejecting malformed input, which is routine
Running out of memory while allocating
A constructor that cannot acquire its resource
A broken class invariant detected in a member function
questions.explanation: Expected, frequent failures belong in the return type, where the caller must look at them. Exceptions suit rare failures the local code cannot handle.

questions.topic: Values or Errors: optional, variant and expected
questions.prompt: Why are exceptions avoided on a latency-critical hot path?
options: They are forbidden by the standard since C++20
A throw is slow and its latency is unpredictable
They leak memory when thrown across threads
They disable inlining for the whole program
questions.explanation: The no-throw path is cheap, but actually throwing takes orders of magnitude longer than a return and varies from call to call. Hot paths report errors with return values.

questions.topic: Values or Errors: optional, variant and expected
questions.prompt: What is the main point of a "vocabulary type" such as `std::optional`?
options: It is usually faster than a raw pointer, because it never allocates
It puts the contract (absent, one of several, value or error) in the signature
It removes the need for templates in generic code, replacing them with variants
It stores its value on the heap so that several owners can share it
questions.explanation: These types replace magic values (`-1`), tagged unions and pointer-plus-count pairs. The meaning is in the type, not in a comment. They are ordinary value types: no heap allocation, no virtual functions.

questions.topic: Values or Errors: optional, variant and expected
questions.prompt: What happens when you write `*opt` on an empty `std::optional<int>`?
options: It throws std::bad_optional_access, like value()
It returns a default-constructed int, which is 0
Undefined behaviour: operator* does not check
It does not compile for an empty optional
questions.explanation: `operator*` and `operator->` are unchecked, like dereferencing a null pointer. `value()` is the checked version and throws `bad_optional_access`; `value_or(x)` supplies a default.

questions.topic: Values or Errors: optional, variant and expected
questions.prompt: How big is `std::optional<int>` compared with `int` (typical 64-bit platform)?
options: The same size: the flag is stored somewhere else
Bigger: the value plus a flag, padded (8 bytes)
Pointer sized, because the value lives on the heap
It depends on the value stored inside
questions.explanation: The int lives inside the optional next to a flag (compiled: 4 versus 8 bytes). There is no heap allocation, which is the main advantage over a pointer or `unique_ptr`.

questions.topic: Values or Errors: optional, variant and expected
questions.prompt: A lookup function may legitimately find nothing, and the reason is obvious. What is the best return type?
options: An `int` that returns -1
A raw pointer that is null when nothing is found, owned by the callee
`std::optional<T>`
It throws an exception on each miss
questions.explanation: `optional<T>` makes "not found" part of the type, needs no allocation and cannot be mistaken for a real value. An exception is too heavy for an expected miss, and a magic value hides the contract.

questions.topic: Values or Errors: optional, variant and expected
questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.code:
std::variant<int, std::string> v;
std::cout << v.index();
options: It is valueless, so index() throws an exception
It does not compile: there is no default constructor
questions.explanation: A default-constructed variant holds a value-initialized first alternative, so `index()` is 0 (the int, value 0). To make "no alternative" the default, put `std::monostate` first.

questions.topic: Values or Errors: optional, variant and expected
questions.prompt: What happens at `std::get<std::string>(v)` when `v` currently holds an `int`?
questions.code:
std::variant<int, std::string> v = 7;
auto s = std::get<std::string>(v);
options: Undefined behaviour, like a union
It throws `std::bad_variant_access`
It converts the int to a string
It returns an empty string
questions.explanation: Unlike a raw union, a variant knows its active alternative, so a wrong `get` is detected and throws. `std::get_if<std::string>(&v)` returns a null pointer instead of throwing.

questions.topic: Values or Errors: optional, variant and expected
questions.prompt: You add a third alternative to a `variant` and forget to handle it in one `std::visit` call that uses `overloaded{...}` lambdas. What happens?
options: It silently skips the new alternative at run time
A compile error: the visitor must accept every alternative
A run-time exception when that alternative is active
The first lambda is called for it by default
questions.explanation: `std::visit` requires the callable to accept every alternative. A missing case is a compile-time error, which is the main safety advantage over a chain of `if` / `get_if` checks or a `switch` on a tag.

questions.topic: Values or Errors: optional, variant and expected
questions.prompt: When is `std::variant` a better fit than a class hierarchy with virtual functions?
options: When the set of types is open and others will add their own
When the set of types is closed and operations keep being added
When speed matters: virtual functions are faster than variants
Only for built-in types such as int and double
questions.explanation: With a closed set of types (messages, tokens, syntax-tree nodes), a variant stores values inline with no allocation or virtual call, and each new operation is one new visitor that the compiler checks for completeness. Virtual functions fit an open set of types.

questions.topic: Values or Errors: optional, variant and expected
questions.prompt: What does `std::expected<T, E>` offer that `std::optional<T>` does not?
options: It stores its value on the heap, not inline, so it can be moved cheaply
It carries the reason for a failure (an E) when there is no T
It has been in the standard library since C++11, in <utility>
It cannot throw, even from value(), so it is noexcept
questions.explanation: `optional` says only "no value". `expected<T, E>` (C++23) holds either the value or an error object that explains what went wrong, without an exception. `value()` on an error still throws `bad_expected_access`.

questions.prompt: What is the value category of the expression `std::move(x)`?
options: lvalue
prvalue
xvalue
It is not an expression
questions.explanation: An xvalue is an object marked as movable, and `std::move` produces one. A prvalue is an unnamed temporary like `5` or `a + b`. "Rvalue" means a prvalue or an xvalue.

questions.prompt: Which expression is a prvalue?
options: `x` (a named variable)
`std::move(x)`
questions.explanation: `x + 1` is an unnamed temporary: a prvalue. `x` and `v[0]` are lvalues; `std::move(x)` is an xvalue.

questions.prompt: Which overload is called?
options: h(const std::string&), because s is an lvalue inside g
h(std::string&&), because s has an rvalue reference type
Neither: the call is ambiguous between the two
The code does not compile
questions.explanation: A name is always an lvalue, whatever its declared type. To pass it on as an rvalue you need `std::move(s)`.

questions.prompt: What can bind to an rvalue reference parameter `T&&`?
options: Any lvalue of type T
Only rvalues: temporaries and std::move(x)
Only const objects of type T
Anything, including lvalues, just like const T&
questions.explanation: An rvalue reference binds to rvalues, which is how overload resolution sends temporaries to move operations. An lvalue needs `std::move` first.

questions.prompt: Which of these is an lvalue?
options: `a + b` for two ints
`std::string("x")`
questions.explanation: An element of a vector has a name path and an address. The others are temporaries.

questions.prompt: Why does `int* p = &5;` not compile?
options: 5 is a temporary and has no address
5 is a constant that lives in read-only memory
Pointers cannot point to ints
& can only be applied to variables of type int
questions.explanation: An rvalue has no stored location you can name. Only lvalues have addresses.

questions.prompt: A function has overloads `f(const std::string&)` and `f(std::string&&)`. Which is called for `f(std::string("b"))`?
options: The `&&` overload
The `const&` overload, because it accepts everything
Neither: the call is ambiguous
Both, one after the other
questions.explanation: An rvalue prefers the rvalue-reference overload when both are viable.

questions.prompt: Which reference type can bind to both lvalues and rvalues?
options: `const T&`
`T&&` on a non-template parameter
`volatile T&`
questions.explanation: A const lvalue reference accepts temporaries. T& rejects them and a plain T&& rejects lvalues.

questions.prompt: Inside `void g(std::string&& s)`, what is the value category of the expression `s`?
options: An lvalue
An rvalue, because of its type
An xvalue
A prvalue
questions.explanation: A name is always an lvalue, whatever its type. Write std::move(s) to treat it as an rvalue again.

questions.prompt: What does `f(s)` call inside `void g(std::string&& s)` when f has `const&` and `&&` overloads?
options: The `const&` overload
The `&&` overload
Neither
It does not compile
questions.explanation: s is an lvalue inside g, so the lvalue overload is chosen.

questions.prompt: What is the type of `decltype((std::move(x)))` for an int x?
options: `int&&`
`int&`
`int`
`const int&`
questions.explanation: std::move gives an xvalue, which decltype with double parentheses reports as T&&.

questions.prompt: What does a parameter of type `const T&&` usually indicate?
options: Almost nothing useful: a const object cannot be moved from
A forwarding reference
A function that steals the argument
A parameter that must be an lvalue
questions.explanation: You cannot steal from a const object, so a const rvalue reference is rarely right.

questions.prompt: What does `std::move(x)` do?
options: Moves x's data to a new memory location and clears the old one for good
Casts x to an rvalue reference so a move can be chosen; it moves nothing
Deletes x so that it can no longer be used by the rest of the program
Copies x into a temporary and then clears the original object afterwards
questions.explanation: `std::move` is just `static_cast<T&&>(x)`. The actual transfer happens in whichever move constructor or move assignment operator is then selected.

questions.prompt: After `std::vector<int> b = std::move(a);`, what may you safely do with `a`?
options: Read a[0]
Call a.size() and trust it equals the old size
Destroy it or assign a new value to it
Not even destroy it, since the program is undefined
questions.explanation: A moved-from object is valid but unspecified: it is safe to destroy or assign to, but you should not rely on its contents.

questions.prompt: What does copying a `std::vector<int>` of a million elements do?
options: Allocates a new buffer and copies every element
Copies only the pointer and the size to the new vector
Shares the buffer until one of the vectors is modified
Moves the buffer and leaves the source vector empty
questions.explanation: A vector copy is deep. A move is the operation that copies only the internals.

questions.prompt: For which type is a move noticeably cheaper than a copy?
options: `std::string` holding a long text
`int`, the plain built-in integer type
A struct made of two plain double values
