A compile error
A double delete
questions.explanation: A cycle leaks silently. A leak checker or a missing destructor message reveals it.

questions.prompt: What does `w.lock()` return when the object is gone?
options: An empty `shared_ptr`
A dangling `shared_ptr`
It throws `bad_weak_ptr`
A raw null pointer of type T*
questions.explanation: lock() never throws and never dangles: it returns an owner or an empty pointer. (Constructing a shared_ptr from an expired weak_ptr throws.)

questions.prompt: Why is `if (!w.expired()) w.lock()->use();` a bug?
options: The owner can vanish between the two calls
expired() is far too slow for this check
lock() cannot be called after expired() was used
It leaks the object that lock() returns
questions.explanation: Call lock() once, test the result and use that owner.

questions.prompt: In a parent that owns its children, which link should be a `weak_ptr`?
options: The child's pointer back to its parent
The parent's pointers to its children
Both of the links between them
Neither of the links between them
questions.explanation: The owning direction stays strong; the back link observes only, which avoids the cycle.

questions.prompt: A cache stores `weak_ptr`s to its entries. What does that achieve?
options: Entries in use are shared and unused ones can be freed
Entries are never freed while the cache exists
Entries are copied again on every single lookup
Entries automatically become thread safe objects
questions.explanation: The cache does not own the entries, so it never keeps an unused one alive.

questions.prompt: A `weak_ptr` is the last reference to an object made with `make_shared`. What is still allocated?
options: The memory block holding the control block
Nothing at all, because the object was destroyed
A second copy of the object that was destroyed
Only the weak_ptr variable itself on the stack
questions.explanation: The destructor ran, but object and control block share one allocation that is freed with the last weak reference.

questions.prompt: What does a `weak_ptr` keep alive?
options: Only the control block
The object it points to
All of the shared owners
Nothing at all, not even the counts
questions.explanation: It must keep the counts so expired() can answer; it never keeps the object.

questions.topic: Threads: The Mental Model and Your First Thread
questions.prompt: What do the threads of one process share, and what does each thread have of its own?
options: They share nothing and communicate only through operating-system pipes
They share the heap and globals; each has its own stack and registers
They share the stack; each thread has its own private heap
They share registers; each has its own heap and its own globals
questions.explanation: Sharing the address space is what makes threads cheap to communicate but dangerous: any shared mutable data needs synchronization.

questions.topic: Threads: The Mental Model and Your First Thread
questions.prompt: What happens when this program runs?
options: It exits normally and the thread is cleaned up by the runtime
std::terminate is called: the thread is still joinable when destroyed
The thread is joined automatically by the thread destructor
It fails to compile because the thread object is never joined
questions.explanation: A `std::thread` must be joined or detached before destruction. Otherwise the destructor calls `std::terminate`. (C++20 `std::jthread` joins automatically.)

questions.topic: Threads: The Mental Model and Your First Thread
questions.prompt: What is the problem with this code?
options: Nothing is wrong: x is passed to the thread by reference
It does not compile: arguments are copied, so pass std::ref(x)
x is incremented twice by the thread before it ends
It leaks the thread object when the function returns
questions.explanation: `std::thread` copies its arguments into internal storage and passes them as rvalues, which cannot bind to `int&`. Write `std::thread t(inc, std::ref(x));`.

questions.topic: Threads: The Mental Model and Your First Thread
questions.prompt: What is the bug here?
options: There is no bug in this code; the thread finishes first
The detached thread may use local after f() returns and destroys it
detach is not allowed with lambda expressions as thread bodies
The thread never starts running because it was detached
questions.explanation: Capturing by reference and detaching lets the thread outlive the variable. Capture by value, or join before returning.

questions.topic: Threads: The Mental Model and Your First Thread
questions.prompt: What is the problem with this code?
options: Nothing: arguments are converted on the calling thread first, so it is safe
The char* is copied and converted to std::string in the new thread, too late
detach cannot be used with a free function as the thread body
buffer is far too large to be copied into a new thread safely
questions.explanation: The thread constructor copies the arguments as given, and the conversion to the parameter type happens later, in the new thread. Convert first: `std::thread t(f, 1, std::string(buffer));`.

questions.topic: Threads: The Mental Model and Your First Thread
questions.prompt: Why does the destructor of a joinable `std::thread` call `std::terminate` instead of joining or detaching for you?
options: Implicit join hides long waits, implicit detach leaves a thread using dead locals
Joining inside a destructor is not possible in standard C++, so it was left out
Calling detach in a destructor is forbidden by the C++ standard, so it terminates
It lets the runtime start threads a little faster than it otherwise could
questions.explanation: Both implicit options have worse failure modes (hard-to-find performance problems, or undefined behavior). Make the thread unjoinable on every path with an RAII guard, or use `std::jthread` in C++20.

questions.topic: Threads: The Mental Model and Your First Thread
questions.prompt: What is the difference between concurrency and parallelism?
options: Parallel tasks run at the same instant; concurrent ones may take turns
They are two names for exactly the same thing
Concurrency needs several cores, but parallelism does not need them
Parallelism is only possible when you use separate processes
questions.explanation: Concurrency is about tasks being in progress together. Parallelism is about running at the same instant.

questions.topic: Threads: The Mental Model and Your First Thread
questions.prompt: For a CPU-bound job, about how many threads make sense?
options: About one per hardware thread
As many threads as there are tasks to do
Always exactly one thread, whatever the machine
Ten times the number of cores on the machine
questions.explanation: More threads than cores only adds context switches. Waiting-bound work can use more.

questions.topic: Threads: The Mental Model and Your First Thread
questions.prompt: What happens if a joinable `std::thread` is destroyed?
options: `std::terminate` is called
It is joined automatically
It is detached automatically
Nothing: the thread just stops
questions.explanation: The standard chose termination over a silent join or detach.

questions.topic: Threads: The Mental Model and Your First Thread
questions.prompt: How do you pass a variable by reference to a `std::thread` function?
options: Wrap it in `std::ref`
Pass it normally
Use a pointer to a pointer
Declare it volatile
questions.explanation: Arguments are copied into the thread; std::ref passes a reference.

questions.topic: Threads: The Mental Model and Your First Thread
questions.prompt: What does a ThreadGuard-style RAII class guarantee?
options: The thread is joined however the scope is left
The thread never gets the chance to start running
The thread is detached as soon as it is created
The thread runs faster than an unguarded thread
questions.explanation: The destructor joins on every path.

questions.topic: Threads: The Mental Model and Your First Thread
questions.prompt: What is the danger of detaching a thread that captured a local by reference?
options: The thread may use the local after it is destroyed
The thread cannot start because of the reference capture
The local variable is copied twice by the lambda
The thread is joined twice when the scope ends
questions.explanation: A detached thread can outlive the function and write to a dead variable.

questions.prompt: Two threads each execute the function below on the same global `counter`, then both are joined. What is true?
questions.code:
int counter = 0;
void work() { for (int i = 0; i < 1000; ++i) ++counter; }
options: counter is always 2000, since both loops run to completion
A data race (undefined behavior); the result may be below 2000
counter is always 1000, because only one thread wins
It does not compile, since counter is not atomic
questions.explanation: `++counter` is load, add, store. Interleavings lose updates, and the unsynchronised concurrent write is formally undefined behavior.

questions.prompt: Which of these is thread-safe without any extra synchronization?
options: Two threads calling `push_back` on the same `std::vector`
Many threads only reading from the same const `std::vector`
One thread writing and another reading the same `int`
Two threads writing to the same `std::string`
questions.explanation: Concurrent reads of data nobody modifies are safe. Any concurrent write plus access needs synchronization, including `push_back` on a standard container.

questions.prompt: Why can `++counter` lose an update when two threads run it?
options: It is three steps
It is slower than a plain addition
Integers cannot be shared
The compiler removes it
questions.explanation: If both threads load before either stores, one increment is lost.

questions.prompt: Which statement about a data race is correct?
options: It is undefined behavior even if the output looks right
It only ever causes you to read a stale value
It needs three or more threads before it can occur
It cannot happen at all when there is only one core
questions.explanation: The compiler assumes there are none, so the program has no defined meaning.

questions.prompt: What is an invariant?
options: A condition on shared data that holds between operations
A variable that is declared once and never changes
A lock that a thread holds for its whole lifetime
A constant expression evaluated by the compiler
questions.explanation: Updates break it briefly, and a reader in the middle sees a broken state.

questions.prompt: How does a race condition differ from a data race?
options: It depends on timing
It is the same thing
It only involves deadlock
It needs a mutex
questions.explanation: A data race is one specific kind of race condition: unsynchronized access.

questions.prompt: Which is the best way to be safe with shared data when it is possible?
options: Do not share
Use a global lock
Make everything volatile
Use more threads
questions.explanation: No sharing means no races and no waiting.

questions.prompt: Is it safe for many threads to read the same `const` object at the same time?
options: Yes, as long as nobody modifies it
No, even read-only access is never safe
Only if every reader takes a mutex first
Only when the program runs on a single core
questions.explanation: Read-only sharing has no conflicting writes.

questions.prompt: What does the thread simulator in this lesson show?
options: That an interleaving of load, add
That mutexes are slow
That atomics are unsafe
That threads always finish in order
questions.explanation: Stepping A and B alternately reproduces the lost increment.

questions.prompt: Why can a real race survive testing for a long time?
options: The bad interleaving may occur once in thousands of runs
Races only exist in debug builds, never in release
The operating system prevents them while tests run
Tests always run on one core so races cannot happen
questions.explanation: Timing-dependent bugs are rare and shift with load.

questions.prompt: Four threads each add into their own slot of `part[t]`. Why is that safe?
options: No two threads write the same memory
The compiler adds a lock
Arrays are atomic
The slots are volatile
questions.explanation: Disjoint writes are not a data race. Merge after join.

questions.prompt: Which change makes that counter correct?
options: Declare the counter as volatile int so that reads are fresh
Declare std::atomic<int> counter (or protect it with a mutex)
Declare the work function inline so the loop is optimized
Join the threads in the opposite order to avoid overlap
questions.explanation: `volatile` gives neither atomicity nor ordering. An atomic makes each increment indivisible; a mutex serialises the critical section.

questions.prompt: Why prefer `std::lock_guard` over calling `m.lock()` and `m.unlock()` yourself?
options: It is faster than calling lock and unlock by hand each time
It unlocks automatically (RAII), even on early return or exception
It allows the same thread to lock the same mutex recursively
It avoids the need for a mutex object altogether
questions.explanation: If code between `lock()` and `unlock()` throws or returns, a manual unlock is skipped and every other thread blocks forever.

questions.prompt: Every member function of this shared stack locks a mutex internally. Why is the caller's code still racy?
options: The mutex is not recursive, so the calls block each other here
Each call is atomic but the sequence is not
lock_guard cannot protect a std::stack from concurrent use
empty() must be called twice before the result can be trusted fully
questions.explanation: This is a check-then-act race built into the interface. The cure is to change the interface, not to add more locking inside the individual calls.

questions.prompt: What is the best fix for that stack?
options: Declare every method of the stack volatile to publish changes
Provide one try_pop() that checks, reads and removes under one lock
Call empty() twice to be sure that the stack has elements
Call notify_all() after each pop to wake the other threads
questions.explanation: Offer whole operations rather than steps, so callers never need to check and act separately. `empty()` may remain as a hint, but its answer can be stale the moment it returns.

questions.prompt: What happens if one thread locks a plain `std::mutex` a second time without unlocking it in between?
options: The second lock is ignored and the thread continues
Undefined behaviour, in practice usually a deadlock
It always throws std::system_error from the second lock
It waits for a timeout and then continues running
questions.explanation: A `std::mutex` is not re-lockable. Only `std::recursive_mutex` lets the owning thread lock again, which is usually a sign of a design problem.

questions.prompt: A public method `depositTwice()` locks a mutex and calls the public `deposit()`, which locks the same mutex. What is the cleaner fix than a `recursive_mutex`?
options: Declare the shared data volatile so the changes become visible everywhere
Split into a locking public method and a private helper that assumes the lock
Make the mutex static so that it is shared by every call to the class
Unlock the mutex just before calling deposit() from depositTwice()
questions.explanation: The locking public method calls a private `...Locked()` function that both public methods share. The lock is taken exactly once and the contract is explicit.

questions.prompt: When does a `std::shared_mutex` pay off compared with a plain `std::mutex`?
options: Whenever there are two or more threads in the program
When many threads read for a while and writes are rare
When the critical section is a single increment of a counter
When threads must run in a fixed, predictable order
questions.explanation: It costs more per lock than a `mutex`, so it only helps when readers dominate and each read holds the lock long enough to overlap with others.

questions.prompt: What does `std::call_once(flag, fn)` guarantee when eight threads call it at the same time?
options: fn runs once for each calling thread, one after the other
fn runs exactly once; the other callers wait until it has finished
fn may run twice, but never more often than that in total
Nothing: you still need a mutex around the call as well
questions.explanation: It is the standard thread-safe one-time initialization. The other threads block until the first call returns, then continue with the initialized state.

questions.prompt: Why prefer `std::lock_guard` to calling `m.lock()` and `m.unlock()`?
options: It unlocks on every path
It is faster
It allows recursive locking
It works without a mutex
questions.explanation: RAII guarantees the unlock, even on early return or exception.

questions.prompt: What should NOT be done while holding a lock?
options: Slow work such as file I/O or sleeping
Reading the shared data that the lock protects
Updating the shared data that the lock protects
Restoring the invariant before the lock is released
questions.explanation: Everything under the lock blocks other threads, so keep it short.

questions.prompt: Which gives the shortest critical section?
options: Compute outside, lock only
Lock for the whole function
Lock before computing
Lock for printing as well
questions.explanation: Lock only the shared access.

questions.prompt: A class locks a mutex inside each method. Is a sequence of two calls safe?
options: No: the invariant between the two calls is unprotected
Yes: each individual method is locked, so the pair is too
Yes, as long as the methods are all declared const
Only on x86, which orders every memory operation
questions.explanation: A caller's sequence is not atomic; offer whole operations.

questions.prompt: When does a `std::shared_mutex` pay off?
options: Many readers and rare writers
Many writers
Only one thread
Short critical sections of one line
questions.explanation: Readers share the lock; writers are exclusive.

questions.prompt: Why is `std::recursive_mutex` often a design smell?
options: It hides code that re-enters with a broken invariant
It is slower than every other kind of mutex
It cannot be unlocked once it has been locked
It does not exist at all before C++20
questions.explanation: Re-locking is usually a sign of a design problem, not a fix.

questions.prompt: Why is `if (!s.empty()) s.pop()` unsafe even if both calls lock?
options: Another thread can empty it between the two calls
empty() is far too slow to call under a lock
pop() requires its own separate lock_guard object
It does not compile with a stack or a queue
questions.explanation: Offer a single operation such as tryPop.

questions.prompt: Thread A locks `m1` then `m2`. Thread B locks `m2` then `m1`. What can happen, and what is the best fix?
options: Nothing: mutexes are fair, so the threads simply take turns
Deadlock; fix with a fixed lock order or std::scoped_lock(m1, m2)
A data race; fix by declaring the protected data volatile
Starvation; fix by lowering one thread's priority a little
questions.explanation: Each holds one lock and waits for the other: circular wait. Locking in the same order everywhere, or locking both at once with `scoped_lock`/`std::lock`, removes the cycle.

questions.prompt: Which of these is NOT one of the four conditions required for a deadlock?
options: Mutual exclusion: only one thread may hold the resource
Hold and wait: a thread holds one lock while requesting another
Circular wait: a cycle of threads each waiting for the next
All locks must be recursive so a thread can re-enter them
questions.explanation: The four Coffman conditions are mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, and circular wait. Breaking any one of them prevents deadlock.

questions.prompt: Can two threads deadlock without any mutex being involved?
options: No: deadlock always needs at least one mutex to be involved somewhere
Yes: for example each thread joins the other, or waits in a future cycle
Only with atomics, when two threads spin waiting on each other
Only if one of the two threads has been detached earlier
questions.explanation: Deadlock is a cycle of waiting. The guideline is general: do not wait for another thread if there is a chance it is waiting for you.

questions.prompt: What does a lock hierarchy (levels on mutexes) give you?
options: Faster locking than a plain mutex, thanks to cached lock levels
A thread may lock only lower levels than it holds, so cycles cannot form
Automatic unlocking at the end of the enclosing scope, like RAII
Fair scheduling between the threads that wait for the same lock
questions.explanation: Runtime-checked ordering turns a rare, timing-dependent deadlock into a deterministic error you can find in testing.

questions.prompt: Why should you not call user-supplied code (a callback, a virtual function) while holding a lock?
options: It may take another lock or keep a pointer to the data
It is always slower than calling your own code
It cannot be copied into the critical section
It must always be declared noexcept to be called
questions.explanation: You do not control what that code does. Never pass out references to protected data, and avoid holding a lock across calls to code you do not own.

questions.prompt: Which is NOT one of the four conditions for a deadlock?
options: Priority inversion
Mutual exclusion
Hold and wait
Circular wait
questions.explanation: The four are mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption and circular wait.

questions.prompt: What does a cycle in the wait-for graph mean?
options: A deadlock
A livelock
A race
A spurious wakeup
questions.explanation: Each thread in the cycle waits for the next one forever.

questions.prompt: How does a global lock order prevent deadlock?
options: It removes the circular wait
It removes mutual exclusion
It makes locks faster
It allows preemption
questions.explanation: If everyone takes a before b, no cycle can form.

questions.prompt: What does `std::scoped_lock lk(a, b)` do?
options: Locks both mutexes with a deadlock-avoidance algorithm
Locks a first and b second strictly in that order
Locks only the first mutex and ignores the second
Detaches the threads that are waiting for the locks
questions.explanation: The argument order does not matter.

questions.prompt: Why should you not call user-supplied code under a lock?
options: It may take another lock or keep a pointer to the protected data
It is slower
It cannot be copied
It must be noexcept
questions.explanation: A callback can create new lock orders or leak references.

questions.prompt: Threads keep reacting to each other and use 100% CPU but make no progress. What is it?
options: Livelock
Deadlock
A data race
Starvation
questions.explanation: A deadlock is idle; a livelock is busy.

questions.prompt: How is livelock usually cured?
options: Randomize the retry delay or impose an order
Add more threads so that somebody makes progress
Switch the mutexes to recursive mutexes everywhere
Declare the shared variables volatile instead
questions.explanation: Breaking the symmetry lets one thread win.

questions.prompt: In a hung program all threads are blocked inside `lock()` and the CPU is at 0%. What is the likely problem?
options: A deadlock
A livelock
A data race
A busy wait
questions.explanation: Idle CPU with every thread waiting points to a deadlock or a lost wakeup.

questions.prompt: Why must `condition_variable::wait` be used with a predicate (or in a loop)?
options: It makes wait faster by skipping the lock on the first check
Wake-ups can be spurious, and the condition may change again
The operating system refuses to wait without a predicate
Without a predicate, wait never returns to the caller
questions.explanation: `cv.wait(lk, pred)` is shorthand for `while (!pred()) cv.wait(lk);`. A bare `wait` can return with the condition still false.

questions.prompt: Why does `condition_variable::wait` take a `std::unique_lock` rather than a `std::lock_guard`?
options: unique_lock is faster than lock_guard in most situations
wait must unlock the mutex while sleeping, then relock on wake-up
lock_guard cannot lock a mutex, only adopt one
It is only a naming convention and either type would work
questions.explanation: Unlocking while the thread sleeps is what lets the producer enter. `lock_guard` has no unlock operation.

questions.prompt: What is a "lost wakeup"?
options: The operating system forgetting a waiting thread in its queue
A notification sent before the waiter slept, so it sleeps forever
A thread being woken up twice for one single event
A mutex being unlocked twice by mistake in the code
questions.explanation: Changing the condition under the mutex makes "check, then sleep" atomic with respect to the update, which closes the window in which a notification can be missed.

questions.prompt: When is `notify_all()` needed instead of `notify_one()`?
options: Never: notify_one is always enough
When several waiters can proceed, or at shutdown to wake everyone
Only when the waiting threads also use atomic variables for data
Only when the shared queue happens to be empty at that moment
questions.explanation: `notify_one` wakes just one thread. For broadcast conditions such as "stop requested", all waiters must be woken.

questions.prompt: Is initialization of a function-local `static` variable thread-safe in C++11 and later?
options: No: you must always add a mutex yourself around the static variable
Yes: it runs exactly once even if several threads reach it together
Only for primitive types such as int and double, not for classes
Only if the static variable is declared const as well
questions.explanation: This "magic statics" guarantee is why the Meyers Singleton needs no explicit locking for its construction.

questions.prompt: How can you detect data races in a C++ program?
options: Add more print statements to the code and rerun it often
Compile with ThreadSanitizer
Use -O3 so the compiler reorders the accesses safely
Declare every shared variable volatile
questions.explanation: ThreadSanitizer instruments memory accesses and reports conflicting unsynchronised accesses with stack traces. Helgrind and DRD help with lock-order issues.

questions.prompt: Why can several threads printing with `std::cout << a << b << '\n'` produce garbled lines?
options: cout cannot be used from several threads at the same time
Each << is a separate operation, so output from threads can interleave
cout is buffered, which reorders the lines between the threads
False sharing corrupts the internal output buffer of the stream
questions.explanation: The stream itself does not crash, but the pieces of different lines mix. Build the full string first and write it once, or protect output with a mutex.

questions.prompt: Why does `cv.wait` take a `std::unique_lock`?
options: It unlocks the mutex while the thread sleeps and relocks it
lock_guard is deprecated and no longer compiles
It needs two different mutexes at the same time
It stores a copy of the mutex inside the variable
questions.explanation: wait must be able to release and reacquire the lock.

questions.prompt: A waiter is woken but the predicate is false. What should it do?
options: Go back to waiting
Continue with the work anyway
Throw an exception to the caller
Call notify on the condition variable
questions.explanation: A wakeup is only a hint: the predicate decides.

questions.prompt: Why must the condition be changed under the same mutex the waiter uses?
options: A notification can be lost between the check and the sleep
It makes the notify call itself run faster
Because notify cannot be called without a lock
Because the condition is really a kind of mutex
questions.explanation: The check-then-sleep must be atomic with respect to the update.

questions.prompt: When is `notify_all` better than `notify_one`?
options: When waiters wait
Always
Never
Only for producers
questions.explanation: notify_one may wake a thread that cannot use the event.

questions.prompt: In a thread-safe queue, where does the consumer wait?
options: `cv.wait(lk, [&]{ return !q.empty(); })`
In a loop that calls sleep_for repeatedly
On the thread id of the producer thread
On a raw atomic flag that it polls hard
questions.explanation: Sleep on the condition variable with a predicate.

questions.prompt: A notify is sent before the consumer starts waiting. What saves the consumer from sleeping forever?
options: It checks the predicate first and sees the item
The notify is queued by the condition variable
wait always returns once
The producer retries
questions.explanation: A condition variable does not remember notifications; the predicate does.

questions.prompt: What does this code do?
questions.code:
std::async(std::launch::async, slowTask);   // returned future is discarded
doOtherWork();
options: Runs slowTask in the background while doOtherWork runs at the same time
Effectively runs slowTask first: the temporary future waits in its destructor
It does not compile because the returned future is simply discarded
Runs doOtherWork first and slowTask only afterwards, one after the other
questions.explanation: A future from `std::async` blocks in its destructor. Because the temporary is destroyed at the end of the statement, `doOtherWork` only starts after `slowTask` completes. Keep the future in a variable.

questions.prompt: What happens if the function run by `std::async` throws, and you later call `future.get()`?
options: The program terminates immediately
get() rethrows the exception in the calling thread
The exception is silently dropped by the future
get() returns a default-constructed value
questions.explanation: The exception is stored in the shared state and rethrown by `get()`. That makes futures the clean way to propagate errors out of worker threads.

questions.prompt: A `std::promise<int>` is destroyed without `set_value` or `set_exception` ever being called. What does `get()` on its future do?
options: It blocks forever, waiting for a value that never comes
It throws std::future_error with broken_promise
It returns 0, the default value of the int
It terminates the program through std::terminate
questions.explanation: The promise breaks and the future is made ready with an error, so the waiting thread is not left hanging.

questions.prompt: Which type lets several threads wait for the same result?
options: `std::future`
`std::shared_future`
`std::packaged_task`
`std::once_flag`
questions.explanation: `std::future` is move-only and can be read once. A `shared_future` is copyable, so every thread gets its own handle on the same result.

questions.prompt: What does `std::packaged_task<int(int)>` do?
options: Runs a function on a new thread immediately when it is created
Wraps a callable and delivers its result into a future, to run later
Caches the return value of a function for repeated calls to it
Creates a whole thread pool around the given function object
questions.explanation: It is a callable plus a future. A pool queues the task, a worker runs it, and the caller reads the result from the future.

questions.prompt: What happens to an exception thrown inside a plain `std::thread` function that escapes?
options: `std::terminate` is called
It is rethrown in main automatically
It is silently ignored by the library
It is stored so that you can read it later
questions.explanation: A task with a future is the way to carry it back.

questions.prompt: Which launch policy guarantees that `std::async` runs on a new thread?
options: `std::launch::async`
`std::launch::deferred`
The default policy
`std::launch::lazy`
questions.explanation: The default may defer the call until get().

questions.prompt: What does `future::get()` do?
options: Waits for the result and returns it, once
Starts the task if it has not started yet
Returns at once with a copy of the value
Cancels the task and discards its result
questions.explanation: get() blocks until ready and can be called only once.

questions.prompt: What happens at the end of the statement `std::async(std::launch::async, work);` with the result discarded?
options: The temporary future blocks until work() finishes
work() is cancelled before it has finished
The program terminates with an error message
work() keeps running quietly in the background
questions.explanation: The future from async waits in its destructor.

questions.prompt: Where is an exception thrown inside an `async` task rethrown?
options: From `future::get()`
From the `async` call
In the worker thread again
Nowhere
questions.explanation: The exception is stored in the shared state and rethrown by get().

questions.prompt: What does a `std::promise` give you?
options: The writing end of a one-shot channel to a future
A second thread that runs your function for you
A mutex that protects the shared result value
A repeating signal that you can send many times
questions.explanation: set_value or set_exception once.

questions.prompt: What does the future see if the promise is destroyed without a value?
options: A `broken_promise` exception
A default constructed value of the type
It waits forever without ever returning
A null pointer that the caller must check
questions.explanation: The library reports the broken promise instead of waiting forever.

questions.prompt: What does `wait_for` return when the task has not finished within the time?

It throws an exception to the caller
It cancels the task and returns the status

questions.topic: Thread Pools, Coordination and Parallel Algorithms
questions.prompt: In a thread pool worker loop, why is the task executed after releasing the queue mutex?

Otherwise the lock is held during the task, so only one task runs at a time
A mutex cannot be locked twice by the same worker thread in a row
Tasks must never use any locks of their own while they are running

questions.topic: Thread Pools, Coordination and Parallel Algorithms
questions.prompt: About how many worker threads should a pool for purely CPU-bound tasks have?

About std::thread::hardware_concurrency(), the core count
Exactly 100, as a round and reasonable number
Always exactly 1, so that tasks never overlap

questions.topic: Thread Pools, Coordination and Parallel Algorithms

The pool grows automatically to make room for the subtasks
The subtasks run first, so everything finishes normally

questions.topic: Thread Pools, Coordination and Parallel Algorithms
questions.prompt: How does work stealing reduce lock contention compared with one shared queue?

Each worker pops its own deque; only idle workers steal from others
It removes the need for any synchronization between workers
It sorts the tasks by size before running any of them
questions.explanation: Owners and thieves work at opposite ends of per-worker deques. The common case touches only local data, and stealing balances the load.

questions.topic: Thread Pools, Coordination and Parallel Algorithms
questions.prompt: How many worker threads suit I/O-bound tasks compared with CPU-bound ones?
options: The same number: hardware_concurrency() for every workload
More than the core count, because threads mostly wait
Always exactly one, since I/O is sequential anyway
Fewer than the core count, to save memory on stacks
questions.explanation: A blocked thread does not use a core, so more threads keep the cores busy. For CPU-bound work extra threads only add context switches.

questions.topic: Thread Pools, Coordination and Parallel Algorithms

A barrier is one-shot, while a latch can be reused
A latch is for processes, while a barrier is for threads

questions.topic: Thread Pools, Coordination and Parallel Algorithms
questions.prompt: A `std::counting_semaphore` is created with 2 permits and six threads each `acquire()`, work and `release()`. What is the maximum number of threads working at once?
options: Unspecified
questions.explanation: The semaphore counts permits: two threads get through and the others wait until a permit is released.

questions.topic: Thread Pools, Coordination and Parallel Algorithms
questions.prompt: What is the right way to stop a running `std::jthread`?

Request a stop; the thread checks its stop_token and returns
detach() it and let it keep running until the program ends
Call std::terminate from some other thread to stop just it
questions.explanation: Stopping is cooperative. The destructor of a `jthread` calls `request_stop()` and then joins.

questions.topic: Thread Pools, Coordination and Parallel Algorithms
questions.prompt: Why must the operation given to `std::reduce` be associative?

The library may regroup operands across threads
Only so that the call compiles when an execution policy is given
Because reduce always runs on a graphics card, never on a CPU

questions.topic: Thread Pools, Coordination and Parallel Algorithms

It must be safe to call from several threads at once
It must be both noexcept and constexpr to be accepted
Nothing: the library adds all the locking itself

questions.topic: Thread Pools, Coordination and Parallel Algorithms
questions.prompt: Why does a pool worker release the lock before running the task?
options: Otherwise only one task could run at a time
To avoid a spurious wakeup of other workers
Because a task is never allowed to hold any lock
To make the queue itself take less memory
questions.explanation: The lock protects only the queue.

questions.topic: Thread Pools, Coordination and Parallel Algorithms
questions.prompt: How many workers for a pool of CPU-bound tasks?
options: About `hardware_concurrency()`
As many as there are tasks in the queue
Exactly one, so that tasks never conflict
Ten per core to keep every core busy
questions.explanation: More workers than cores only adds switching.

questions.topic: Thread Pools, Coordination and Parallel Algorithms
questions.prompt: In work stealing, where does an idle worker take a task from?
options: The back of another worker's deque
The front of one shared global queue
Its own deque, from the same end as before
A random thread's stack, chosen by the scheduler

questions.topic: Thread Pools, Coordination and Parallel Algorithms
questions.prompt: How do you safely stop a worker thread?
options: Ask it to stop with a `stop_token`
Kill the thread from outside at any moment
Call detach on it so that it goes away
Destroy the mutex that the worker is using
questions.explanation: There is no safe forced kill in standard C++.

questions.prompt: When is `std::atomic` NOT enough on its own?
options: Incrementing a single shared counter from many threads
A flag that tells a worker thread to stop
An invariant over several variables that must change together
Publishing a pointer to data that is already finished
questions.explanation: Atomics make operations on one variable indivisible. Updating two related variables consistently needs a mutex (or a single atomic holding both).

questions.prompt: Is `volatile` a valid way to share a flag between threads in C++?

No: it gives no atomicity or ordering between threads; use std::atomic
Yes, but only for variables of type bool or char on most targets
Yes, but only on x86 processors with their strong memory ordering
questions.explanation: Concurrent access to a `volatile` variable is still a data race. `volatile` is for memory-mapped hardware, not thread synchronization.

questions.prompt: What does `compare_exchange_weak(expected, desired)` do when the current value is not equal to `expected`?

Returns false and loads the current value into expected
Throws an exception to report the mismatch to the caller
Returns true and leaves expected completely unchanged

questions.prompt: Why is `compare_exchange_weak` normally used inside a loop?
options: It is faster than a mutex, so it is preferred
It may fail spuriously even when the values match
It cannot be called more than once on the same atomic object
It blocks until the swap finally succeeds, like a lock does
questions.explanation: `weak` is allowed to fail spuriously (cheaper on some CPUs). `compare_exchange_strong` fails only on a real mismatch.

questions.prompt: What is the ABA problem?
options: A CAS succeeds because the value is A again, though it went through B
Two threads sharing the same atomic variable at the same moment
A deadlock between two mutexes locked in opposite orders
A compiler bug that is triggered by the volatile keyword
questions.explanation: The value looks unchanged, so the CAS succeeds, but a node may have been freed and reused in between. Fix with a version counter or hazard pointers.

questions.prompt: Which standard atomic type is guaranteed to be lock-free?
options: `std::atomic<std::string>`
`std::atomic_flag`
`std::atomic<std::vector<int>>`
All of them
questions.explanation: `std::atomic_flag` is the only type the standard requires to be lock-free. Others depend on the type and platform (`is_lock_free()`).

questions.prompt: What is the difference between `x++` on an int and on a `std::atomic<int>` shared by two threads?
options: The atomic increment is one indivisible step
The atomic one is slower and still races as before
There is no difference, since both are the same
The plain int increment is atomic on x86 anyway
questions.explanation: An atomic read-modify-write cannot be interleaved.

questions.prompt: What does `compare_exchange` do on failure?
options: Loads the current value into `expected`
Throws an exception that the caller must handle
Stores `desired` anyway, to force the update
Resets the variable to zero so it can start over
questions.explanation: That is what makes the retry loop easy to write.

questions.prompt: When is a spinlock a bad idea?
options: When the lock holder can be descheduled
For very short critical sections of a few lines
On cores that are dedicated to the spinning threads
For protecting a single increment of a counter
questions.explanation: Spinners burn CPU while the holder is not running.

questions.prompt: What does `counter.exchange(9)` return?
options: The previous value
The new value of counter
Nothing
questions.explanation: exchange writes and returns the old value in one step.

questions.prompt: Which operation is NOT made safe by `std::atomic<int>` alone?
options: Keeping two atomics consistent with each other
A single increment of one atomic integer variable
A load of one atomic integer variable
A store to one atomic integer variable

questions.prompt: Why is the `expected` argument passed by reference to `compare_exchange`?
options: A failed attempt can write the current value back into it
To avoid a copy of a large object on each call
So that the function can change the desired value
It is not passed by reference in the standard
questions.explanation: The failure path updates expected so the loop can recompute.

questions.prompt: What does `atomic_flag::test_and_set` return?
options: The previous value of the flag
Whether the flag type is lock-free
The new value
Nothing
questions.explanation: A spinlock loops until it sees that the flag was previously clear.

questions.prompt: Which order is enough for `nextId.fetch_add(1)` used as a unique id generator?
options: `relaxed`
`release`
`acquire`
None: atomics cannot do it
questions.explanation: Only atomicity matters; no other data depends on the value.

questions.topic: The Memory Model: Orders and Happens-Before
questions.prompt: What is the default memory order of `std::atomic` operations, and what does it mean?
options: relaxed: there is no ordering between the threads
seq_cst: one global order for all threads (strongest, simplest)
acquire, which is applied to loads only by default in C++
release, which is applied to stores only by default in C++
questions.explanation: Sequential consistency is the default because it is the easiest to reason about. Weaker orders are an optimisation that needs justification.

questions.topic: The Memory Model: Orders and Happens-Before
questions.prompt: What does this guarantee?
options: It may print 0 or 42, depending on how the threads are scheduled
It prints 42
It is a data race with undefined behavior on the shared data
It prints nothing because the consumer loop never ends
questions.explanation: A release store paired with an acquire load that observes it creates a happens-before edge, so the write to `data` is visible. With relaxed ordering this would not be guaranteed.

questions.topic: The Memory Model: Orders and Happens-Before
questions.prompt: Which pair of orders publishes data written before a store to a thread that reads the stored value?
options: Both operations use relaxed
A release store and an acquire load
An acquire store and a release load
Only volatile reads and writes
questions.explanation: The release store and acquire load synchronize-with each other, so earlier writes happen-before the reader's later reads.

questions.topic: The Memory Model: Orders and Happens-Before
questions.prompt: A producer stores the flag with `release`, but the consumer loads it with `relaxed`. What is guaranteed about the data written before the store?
options: It is visible, because the store was a release operation on the flag
Nothing: without an acquire on the reading side there is no ordering
It is guaranteed visible only if the data is declared volatile
The program does not compile when memory orders are mixed like this
questions.explanation: Both sides must take part. A relaxed load does not synchronize, so reading the data afterwards can be a data race.

questions.topic: The Memory Model: Orders and Happens-Before
questions.prompt: What does "A happens-before B" mean?
options: A starts earlier than B in wall-clock time
A's effects are guaranteed to be visible to B
A and B run on the same processor core
A runs faster than B on the same machine
questions.explanation: It is the memory model's visibility relation: program order within a thread, plus the edges created by synchronization (atomics, mutexes, join, futures).

questions.topic: The Memory Model: Orders and Happens-Before
questions.prompt: Why can code with a wrong memory order seem to work on x86 and fail on ARM?
options: x86 has no caches that could reorder the memory accesses
x86 already gives release/acquire ordering; ARM reorders more
ARM does not support atomic operations
Compilers only optimise code aggressively for ARM targets
questions.explanation: The C++ memory model, not the machine you test on, defines correctness. x86 hides some missing orderings.

questions.topic: The Memory Model: Orders and Happens-Before
questions.prompt: Which orders suit the decrement of a reference count where the thread that drops it to zero deletes the object?
options: relaxed on both the increment and the decrement of the count
acq_rel, so the last thread sees all other writes before deleting
release only, applied to the load of the counter value
No atomic is needed for a reference count in C++
questions.explanation: Increments can be relaxed, but the decrement must acquire what the other owners released before the object is destroyed.

questions.topic: The Memory Model: Orders and Happens-Before
questions.prompt: Which memory order is normally enough for a statistics counter that nothing else depends on?
options: `seq_cst`
`relaxed`
`acquire`
`release`
questions.explanation: Only atomicity is needed: the final total is right and no other data is published through the counter.

questions.topic: The Memory Model: Orders and Happens-Before
questions.prompt: Why does the two-lock queue keep a dummy node?
options: To save memory when the queue is empty most of the time
A push touches only the tail and a pop only the head
To make the queue lock-free without any other change
To keep the elements stored in the queue sorted
questions.explanation: With a permanent dummy node, head and tail never point at the same real node, so each end can have its own mutex.

questions.topic: The Memory Model: Orders and Happens-Before
questions.prompt: Why is a lock-free pop much harder to write than a lock-free push?
options: Pop needs more arguments than push does, so it is slower
Another thread may free the node you read
Pop cannot use atomic operations, so it must use a mutex
Push is not lock-free either in this design, only pop is
questions.explanation: Push only links a node you own. Pop reads and frees nodes other threads may still be using, which needs hazard pointers, epochs or counted pointers.

questions.topic: The Memory Model: Orders and Happens-Before
questions.prompt: What is the difference between lock-free and wait-free?
options: There is no difference between the two terms, both mean lock-free
Lock-free: some thread always progresses; wait-free: all do, in bounded steps
Wait-free algorithms use mutexes to bound the waiting time for threads
Lock-free means that no atomic operations are used by the algorithm
questions.explanation: Wait-free is the stronger guarantee: no thread can be starved indefinitely by others.

questions.topic: The Memory Model: Orders and Happens-Before
questions.prompt: Which of these can reorder memory operations between threads?
options: The compiler, the CPU
Only the compiler
Only the CPU
Only the operating system
questions.explanation: All three layers can change the order another thread observes.

questions.topic: The Memory Model: Orders and Happens-Before
questions.prompt: Which memory order is the default for atomic operations?
options: `memory_order_seq_cst`
`memory_order_relaxed`
`memory_order_acquire`
`memory_order_release`
questions.explanation: The default is the strongest and easiest to reason about.

questions.topic: The Memory Model: Orders and Happens-Before
questions.prompt: Which order suits a statistics counter that nothing else depends on?
options: `relaxed`
`seq_cst`
`release`
`acq_rel`
questions.explanation: Only atomicity of the total is needed.

questions.topic: The Memory Model: Orders and Happens-Before
questions.prompt: Which of these creates a happens-before edge between threads?
options: `join()` on the other thread
Reading a plain int twice
Calling `sleep_for`
Printing with `std::cout`
questions.explanation: Joining synchronizes the end of the thread with the code after join.

questions.topic: The Memory Model: Orders and Happens-Before
questions.prompt: Inside a single thread, what gives happens-before?
options: Program order
The mutex
A memory fence only
Nothing
questions.explanation: Within one thread each statement happens-before the next.

questions.topic: The Memory Model: Orders and Happens-Before
questions.prompt: What goes wrong in double-checked locking without release/acquire?
options: Another thread can see the pointer before the object is built
The mutex deadlocks the first time it is taken
The pointer stays null forever for every thread
The call to new throws an exception each time
questions.explanation: The constructor's writes may not be visible yet.

questions.topic: The Memory Model: Orders and Happens-Before
questions.prompt: Why does a two-lock queue use a dummy node?
options: Pushes touch only the tail
To store the size
To allow reverse iteration
To make the queue lock-free
questions.explanation: The dummy node keeps head and tail from meeting on the same node.

questions.prompt: What is the key difference between `std::string` and `std::string_view`?
options: string_view is faster because it uses vectorised instructions internally
string owns its characters; string_view only points at someone else's
string_view can modify the text in place, which string cannot do
They are the same type under two names; both own their text
questions.explanation: A view is a pointer plus a length with no ownership. It never allocates, but it is only valid while the underlying characters are alive.

questions.prompt: What is wrong with this code?
questions.code:

std::cout << name;
options: It prints temporary without any problem
It does not compile because of the temporary string object
The view dangles: the temporary string dies after the first statement
string_view cannot be printed with cout, only std::string can
questions.explanation: The temporary `std::string` dies at the semicolon, so `name` points at freed memory. Reading it is undefined behaviour.

questions.prompt: Which parameter type is best for a function that only reads text and should accept literals, std::string and substrings without copying?
options: `std::string`
`std::string&`
`const std::string&`
`std::string_view`
questions.explanation: `std::string_view` binds to all of them without allocating. `const std::string&` would build a temporary string for a literal.

questions.prompt: What does `std::string::find` return when the text is not found?
options: `std::string::npos`
It throws `std::out_of_range`
questions.explanation: `find` returns the constant `npos`, a very large unsigned value. Comparing the result to -1 through an `int` is a classic bug.

questions.prompt: Is it safe to pass `sv.data()` of a `std::string_view` to a C function expecting a null-terminated string?
options: Yes: a view is null-terminated, just like a C string
No: a view is not guaranteed to be null-terminated
Yes, but only when the view refers to a string literal
No: a view has no data() member that could be passed on
questions.explanation: A view of a substring does not end in `\0`. Convert to `std::string` first if you need a C string.

questions.prompt: What does `std::regex_match("xabcx", std::regex("abc"))` return?
options: true
false
It throws `std::regex_error`
It returns the position 1
questions.explanation: `regex_match` requires the pattern to match the **entire** string. The extra `x` characters make it fail; `regex_search` would return true.

questions.prompt: Which function finds a match anywhere inside a string and fills a `std::smatch` with the captures?
options: `std::regex_match`
`std::regex_search`
`std::regex_replace`
`std::regex_find`
questions.explanation: `regex_search` looks for the first match anywhere and stores the whole match and each group in the `smatch`. There is no `regex_find`.

questions.prompt: After a successful `regex_search(line, m, std::regex(R"((\w+)=(\d+))"))` on "x=42", what is `m[2]`?
questions.explanation: `m[0]` is the whole match, `m[1]` is the first group (`x`) and `m[2]` is the second group (`42`).

questions.prompt: How do you visit every match in a string, not just the first?
options: Call `regex_search` once; it returns all matches
Use `std::sregex_iterator`
Use `regex_match` in a loop
Use `std::regex_all`
questions.explanation: A `std::sregex_iterator` constructed over the range walks all matches; compare it with a default-constructed iterator to detect the end.

questions.prompt: Why should you not construct a `std::regex` inside a hot loop?
options: It is not thread safe, so concurrent loops corrupt its internal state
Construction compiles the pattern, which is expensive; build it once
It leaks memory each time one is constructed in a loop
The compiler forbids constructing regex objects inside loop bodies
questions.explanation: Pattern compilation happens at construction. Create it once (for example as a `static const`) and reuse it.

questions.prompt: What does an invalid pattern such as `std::regex("(")` do?
options: It silently matches no input and carries on
It throws std::regex_error when constructed
It is rejected by the compiler at compile time
It matches all strings, like an empty pattern
questions.explanation: Patterns are parsed at run time, so an invalid one throws `std::regex_error` when the regex object is built.

questions.prompt: Which clock should you use to measure how long an operation took or to implement a timeout?
options: `system_clock`, because it is the most accurate
`steady_clock`, because it is monotonic
`high_resolution_clock`, since it has the finest tick
The three clocks behave the same for this purpose
questions.explanation: `system_clock` can jump when the system time changes. `steady_clock` never goes backwards, which is what interval measurement needs.

questions.prompt: Which line does NOT compile?
options: Both
Neither
questions.explanation: Converting seconds to milliseconds is lossless so it is implicit. Converting back could lose precision, so it needs an explicit `duration_cast<seconds>(ms)`.

questions.prompt: What does `std::chrono::duration_cast<std::chrono::minutes>(90s).count()` give?
questions.explanation: Integer durations truncate when cast to a coarser unit, so 90 seconds becomes 1 minute.

questions.prompt: What does this statement do?

options: It prints 1 if z is absent, as the expression suggests
It prints 0 if z is absent, as the expression suggests
It does not compile as intended: << binds tighter than ==
It prints npos only when z is absent from the string
questions.explanation: It parses as `(std::cout << s.find('z')) == npos`, comparing a stream with a number. Parenthesise the comparison.

questions.prompt: What is the small string optimisation (SSO)?

Strings are stored in read-only memory by the compiler
The compiler merges duplicate strings into a single shared copy
questions.explanation: A `std::string` has room for a handful of characters (about 15 in libstdc++) inside the object. Longer text goes to the heap.

questions.prompt: Why call `reserve(1000)` before appending 1000 characters one at a time?
options: It makes the string read-only afterwards, which speeds up reads
It allocates once, so appending never reallocates
It removes the null terminator from the buffer to save one byte
It converts the string into a string_view over the same buffer
questions.explanation: Without `reserve`, capacity grows geometrically and each growth copies the characters and invalidates pointers and iterators.

questions.prompt: What happens to a pointer obtained from `s.c_str()` when you append to `s` and it reallocates?
options: It stays valid, since the string owns the memory it points to
It dangles: reallocation moves the characters and invalidates it
It is updated automatically by the string whenever it reallocates
It becomes a null pointer, which is safe to test and ignore
questions.explanation: Any operation that may reallocate invalidates pointers, references and iterators into the string.

questions.prompt: What does `std::from_chars` return for the input "12x4" when parsing an `int`?
options: It throws invalid_argument for the bad input
It parses 12 with no error and leaves ptr at x4
It returns 0 together with an error code
It parses 124, skipping the stray character

questions.prompt: Why is `std::from_chars` preferred over `std::stoi` on a hot path?
options: It is the standard way to parse an int in C++
It does not throw, allocate or use the locale
It is faster because it uses vector instructions
It accepts leading whitespace and plus signs
questions.explanation: `from_chars` reports errors with a return value and works on a character range, so there are no exceptions, no temporary `string` and no locale lookup.

questions.prompt: What is a drawback of `std::cout << std::hex << 255;` compared with `std::format("{:x}", 255)`?
options: It cannot print numbers in hexadecimal, only in decimal
The stream stays in hex mode, so later integers print in hex too
It allocates a temporary string each time it prints a number
It needs C++23 to compile, unlike std::format
questions.explanation: Many stream manipulators are sticky. `std::format` is stateless: the format applies to that one replacement field only.

questions.prompt: Which loop reads a file line by line correctly?

questions.prompt: When is a `std::ofstream` closed if you never call `close()`?
options: Only when you call close() yourself at some point
When its destructor runs at the end of its scope
When the whole program exits normally
When the last line is written to the file
